questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: The annual average effective dose to the U.S. population from all sources of radiation, including background, is approximately:
questions.explanation: The annual average effective dose to the U.S. population from all sources of radiation, including background, is about 620 mrem. This figure serves as a general reference point for contextualizing radiation exposure from medical and other sources.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: The as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) acronym stands for:
questions.explanation: ALARA stands for "as low as reasonably achievable," referring to the judicious use of nuclear radiology imaging such that radiation exposure to the public and personnel is kept as low as possible while still yielding a diagnosis.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: How often must the as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) program be reviewed?
questions.explanation: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) mandates annual review of the ALARA program. This is distinct from the quarterly review of personnel dosimetry records, which is a separate requirement.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: Annual review of the as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) program is the responsibility of which individual?
questions.explanation: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) mandates that annual review of the ALARA program be performed by the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO). While the Radiation Safety Committee (RSC) has broader oversight responsibilities including quarterly review of dosimetry records, the annual ALARA program review is specifically assigned to the RSO.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a required component of a radiation protection program?

choices.text: Training and experience of authorized users
Inventory of sealed sources and leak testing
Record of administered activity for diagnostic and therapeutic procedures
Quarterly inspection of radiopharmaceutical storage areas

questions.explanation: The three required components of a radiation protection program are: training and experience of authorized users, inventory of sealed sources and leak testing, and a record of administered activity for diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. Quarterly inspection of radiopharmaceutical storage areas is not listed as a required component.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: The maximum allowable dose to members of the public from a licensed operation, including hospital staff working outside of a radiology department (e.g., nursing, administration), must not exceed:
questions.explanation: Licensees must ensure that the highest dose to the public shall not exceed 100 mrem/year. This limit explicitly applies to hospital staff working outside of a radiology/imaging department, including administration, support, nursing, engineering, and transport personnel. 5 rem/year is the annual whole-body occupational dose limit for adult radiation workers, not the public limit.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the three primary measures used to decrease radiation exposure to personnel?
questions.explanation: The three primary measures to decrease radiation exposure to personnel are time, shielding, and distance. Dosimetry is an important tool for monitoring radiation exposure but is not one of the three primary protective measures.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: How often must the Radiation Safety Committee review personnel dosimetry records?
questions.explanation: The Radiation Safety Committee (RSC) must review dosimetry records every 3 months. The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) also reviews personnel dosimetry records on this same quarterly basis. Both share this oversight responsibility at the same interval.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: Individual dosimeters are required for personnel whose expected radiation exposures exceed what fraction of the annual occupational dose?
questions.explanation: Individual dosimeters are required if personnel exposures are expected to exceed greater than 10% of the annual occupational dose in a year. This threshold ensures that those with meaningful potential for radiation exposure are formally monitored.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: Planned audits of the radiation protection program must occur at a minimum frequency of:
questions.explanation: Periodic, planned audits must be carried out at least every 12 months to verify compliance with all aspects of the radiation protection program. Results, including any follow-up actions, must be documented and reviewed by hospital/facility administration.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: Who is required to perform audits of the radiation protection program?

choices.text: Trained personnel without direct responsibilities in the area being audited
A member of the radiation safety committee
The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) or their designee

questions.explanation: Audits must be performed by trained personnel not having direct responsibilities in the department or facility being audited. This requirement ensures objectivity and independence in the audit process.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: A "radiation area" is defined as one in which the effective dose could exceed what level in 1 hour at 30 cm from the source?
questions.explanation: A "radiation area" is defined as one where the effective dose could result in an excess of 5 mrem in 1 hour at 30 cm from a radiation source. This threshold distinguishes it from a "high radiation area" (100 mrem in 1 hour at 30 cm) and from unrestricted areas, which must remain below 2 mrem in any 1 hour.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: A "high radiation area" is defined as one in which the effective dose could reach up to what level in 1 hour at 30 cm from the source?
questions.explanation: A "high radiation area" is where the effective dose is up to 100 mrem in 1 hour at 30 cm from the source. By contrast, a "radiation area" threshold is 5 mrem in 1 hour at 30 cm, and a "very high radiation area" is defined by an absorbed dose exceeding 500 rad in 1 hour at 1 meter.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: Which safety feature is specifically required to control access to a high radiation area?
questions.explanation: A visible or audible alarm is required to control access to a high radiation area. This is a specific requirement tied to the high radiation area designation and is not listed as a requirement for standard radiation areas.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: A "very high radiation area" is defined as one where the absorbed dose could exceed what level in 1 hour at 1 meter from the source?
questions.explanation: A "very high radiation area" is defined as one where the absorbed dose levels could exceed 500 rad in 1 hour at 1 meter from the source or from any surface. Note that this threshold is expressed in absorbed dose (rad), not dose equivalent (rem), and is measured at 1 meter rather than the 30 cm used for radiation areas and high radiation areas.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: Unrestricted (public) areas must maintain a dose rate that does not exceed:
questions.explanation: Unrestricted areas must have dose rates less than 2 mrem in any 1 hour, or less than 100 mrem/year. This is lower than the threshold defining a "radiation area" (5 mrem in 1 hour at 30 cm from a source), reflecting the stricter limits applied to areas accessible to the general public.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: A room containing a sealed source is not required to be posted with a caution sign if the radiation level at 30 cm from the source container does not exceed:
questions.explanation: A room or area is not required to be posted with a caution sign in the presence of a sealed source if the radiation level at 30 cm from the source surface container or housing does not exceed 5 mrem per hour. This threshold is consistent with the lower boundary of a "radiation area," below which standard caution posting is not mandated.

questions.chapterName: Section 1: Radiation Protection
questions.stem: The standard radiation symbol authorized by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) uses which color scheme?

choices.text: Yellow or green on a black background
Black or blue on a white background
Magenta, purple, or black on a yellow background
Red or orange on a white background

questions.explanation: The standard radiation symbol authorized by the NRC uses the colors magenta, purple, or black on a yellow background. Licensees are authorized to label sources, source holders, or other device components without a color requirement.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT represent a recognized way to measure radiation?
questions.explanation: The four fundamental ways to measure radiation can be remembered by the mnemonic R-E-A-D: Radioactivity, Exposure, Absorbed dose, and Dose equivalent. Effective dose is a derived quantity calculated from dose equivalent and tissue weighting factors, but it is not one of the four primary measurement categories in this framework.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: How many megabecquerels (MBq) are equivalent to 1 millicurie (mCi)?
questions.explanation: 1 mCi equals 37 MBq. The curie (Ci) and becquerel (Bq) are both units of radioactivity, and this conversion is fundamental to nuclear medicine practice. Knowing it allows for fluent translation between the older conventional unit system (Ci) and the SI unit system (Bq).

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: A type of radiation consisting of two protons and two neutrons, with high linear energy transfer, that travels only 10-100 micrometers in tissue. Which of the following is being described?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are positively charged particles consisting of two protons and two neutrons, making them equivalent to a helium nucleus. They have high LET, causing substantial radiobiological damage to surrounding tissue, but their very short range in tissue (on average only 10-100 micrometers) limits their penetration. Because of this, they pose the greatest risk when internalized through ingestion, inhalation, or direct medical therapeutic use.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: A type of radiation consisting of electrons or positrons emitted from a decaying nucleus, with moderate linear energy transfer, that can be stopped by a few millimeters of plastic. Which of the following is being described?
questions.explanation: Beta particles are electrons (beta-minus) or positrons (beta-plus) emitted from a decaying nucleus. They have moderate LET and greater penetration than alpha particles but can be stopped by a few millimeters of plastic. Beta-minus particles can be used for therapeutic purposes. Beta-plus particles (positrons) are highly reactive and travel only a very short distance before undergoing annihilation with a beta-minus particle.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The beta-minus particle emitted by iodine-131 travels approximately how far in tissue?
questions.explanation: The beta-minus (negatron) particle emitted by I-131 travels approximately 0.5-3.0 mm in tissue. This is considerably farther than alpha particles (which travel only 10-100 micrometers) but far shorter than the penetration range of gamma rays, which can pass through several centimeters of lead. This limited tissue range makes beta emitters well-suited for targeted radiotherapy.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: When a beta-plus particle (positron) undergoes annihilation with a beta-minus particle, what is produced?

choices.text: A burst of alpha particles and low-energy gamma rays
Two 511 keV gamma rays emitted in opposite directions
Two 140 keV gamma rays emitted in opposite directions

questions.explanation: When a positron (beta-plus) travels a very short distance before combining in an annihilation event with a beta-minus particle, two 511 keV gamma rays are ejected in exactly opposite directions (180 degrees apart). This simultaneous dual-photon emission is the physical foundation for positron emission tomography (PET) imaging, which uses coincidence detection of these opposing photons to localize the site of annihilation.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: X-rays, in the context of radiation biology, are produced by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.text: Annihilation of a positron and electron pair
Beta-minus particles undergoing Bremsstrahlung as they pass near high atomic mass nuclei
Isomeric transition of a metastable nucleus
Electron capture by an unstable nucleus

questions.explanation: X-rays in this context are electromagnetic waves with no mass, created when beta-minus particles pass near a high atomic mass nucleus (such as lead or tungsten) and are deflected, emitting low-energy x-rays through Bremsstrahlung (braking) radiation. This is distinct from gamma rays, which are also photons without mass but are emitted directly from the nucleus during radioactive decay.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which type of radiation can penetrate most materials and may induce nuclear reactions in surrounding materials?
questions.explanation: Neutron radiation consists of free neutrons emitted from the breaking apart of an atomic nucleus. Unlike charged particles, neutrons have no charge and can penetrate most shielding materials. They can also cause nuclear reactions in other materials (called chain reactions), which distinguishes them from alpha particles, beta particles, and gamma rays.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The physical half-life of a radionuclide is defined as:

choices.text: The time for 50% of the radionuclide nuclei to undergo radioactive decay
The time for the effective dose from a radionuclide to decrease by 50%
The combined rate of physical decay and biological excretion
The time for biological excretion to reduce the body burden by 50%

questions.explanation: The physical half-life (Tp) is defined as the time it takes for 50% of the radionuclide nuclei to decay. This is a fixed, intrinsic property of the radionuclide and is independent of its chemical form or biological environment. It is distinct from the biological half-life, which reflects excretion from the body, and the effective half-life, which combines both.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The biological half-life of a radiopharmaceutical is defined as:

choices.text: The time for 50% of the radionuclide nuclei to undergo radioactive decay
The time for the radiation dose rate to decrease by half
The combined rate of physical decay and metabolic clearance
The time for the radiopharmaceutical concentration in the body to decrease by 50%

questions.explanation: The biological half-life (Tb) is the time it takes for the radiopharmaceutical concentration within the body to reduce to 50% of the original concentration, reflecting the rate of biological excretion and metabolism. Unlike physical half-life, it is not a fixed property of the radionuclide and can vary based on the patient's physiology and the radiopharmaceutical's chemical form.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The effective half-life of a radiopharmaceutical accounts for which two processes?

choices.text: Physical nuclear decay and biological excretion

questions.explanation: The effective half-life (Te) combines the effects of physical nuclear decay and biological excretion. Because both processes work simultaneously to reduce the amount of radioactive material in the body, the effective half-life is always shorter than either the physical or biological half-life alone. It is calculated as Te = (Tp x Tb) / (Tp + Tb).

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: A radiopharmaceutical has a physical half-life of 6 hours and a biological half-life of 3 hours. What is its effective half-life?
questions.explanation: The effective half-life is calculated using the formula Te = (Tp x Tb) / (Tp + Tb). Substituting the values: Te = (6 x 3) / (6 + 3) = 18 / 9 = 2 hours. The effective half-life is always shorter than either the physical or biological half-life individually because both processes are simultaneously reducing the body burden of the radionuclide.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes "exposure" as a radiation measurement?

choices.text: The amount of energy deposited in tissue by radiation, scaled by tissue mass
The total effective dose equivalent from internal and external sources
The amount of radiation present in the air
The absorbed dose multiplied by a radiation quality factor

questions.explanation: Exposure describes the amount of radiation present in the air, specifically the ionization produced in air by x-ray or gamma radiation. It is measured in Roentgen (R) or coulombs per kilogram (C/kg), with typical instruments reporting in milliRoentgen (mR). A standard chest radiograph produces approximately 10 mR of exposure.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the units used to measure exposure?
questions.explanation: Exposure is measured in Roentgen (R) or coulombs per kilogram (C/kg), and instruments typically report in milliRoentgen (mR). Gray and rad are units of absorbed dose; Sievert and rem are units of dose equivalent; and Becquerel and curie are units of radioactivity.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes "absorbed dose"?

choices.text: The amount of energy deposited in tissue by radiation, scaled by the mass of the tissue
The absorbed dose multiplied by a radiation quality factor to account for biological effectiveness
The sum of effective dose equivalents from all external and internal radiation sources
The ionization produced in air by radiation

questions.explanation: Absorbed dose describes the amount of energy that radiation deposits while passing through tissue, scaled by the mass of the tissue. Because absorbed dose is mass-dependent, the same amount of radiation will produce a greater absorbed dose value in a smaller organ (e.g., kidneys) than in a larger one (e.g., liver). Absorbed dose does not account for differences in the biological effectiveness of different radiation types.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the units of absorbed dose?
questions.explanation: Absorbed dose is expressed in Gray (Gy), the SI unit, or rad (the older conventional unit). The conversion is 100 rads = 1 Gy. Roentgen and C/kg are units of exposure; Sievert and rem are units of dose equivalent; and Becquerel and curie are units of radioactivity.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: How many rads are equivalent to 1 Gray (Gy)?
questions.explanation: 100 rads is equivalent to 1 Gray (Gy), the SI unit of absorbed dose. This is an important conversion analogous to the relationship between rem and Sievert for dose equivalent (100 rem = 1 Sv).

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: For the same total amount of absorbed radiation, which of the following is true regarding absorbed dose in organs of different sizes?

choices.text: Smaller organs receive a greater absorbed dose because the same energy is deposited into less mass
Absorbed dose is the same regardless of organ size
Absorbed dose depends only on the type of radiation, not on organ size
Larger organs receive a greater absorbed dose because they intercept more radiation

questions.explanation: Absorbed dose is defined as the energy deposited per unit mass of tissue. Therefore, for the same amount of deposited energy, a smaller organ will have a higher absorbed dose value than a larger organ. For example, the kidneys would have a greater absorbed dose value than the liver if both received the same total radiation energy.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Linear energy transfer (LET) describes which of the following?

choices.text: The number of ion pairs created per unit path length in air
The ratio of absorbed dose to exposure for a given radiation type
The distance traveled by a particle before it loses all of its energy in tissue
The rate of energy transferred by radiation to a medium per unit of length

questions.explanation: Linear energy transfer (LET) describes the rate of energy transferred by radiation to a medium per unit of length. Radiation with higher LET (such as alpha particles and neutrons) releases energy more densely along its path, causing greater tissue damage per unit of distance traveled, and therefore correlates with higher relative biological effectiveness (RBE).

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following radiation types has the highest linear energy transfer (LET)?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles have the highest LET of the radiation types listed. They deposit energy very densely over a short path, causing substantial radiobiological damage. In contrast, gamma rays, x-rays, and beta particles have lower LET and are less biologically damaging per unit of absorbed dose. The radiation weighting factor reflects this: alpha particles carry a weighting factor of 20, compared to 1 for gamma rays, x-rays, and beta particles.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Dose equivalent is calculated by multiplying the absorbed dose of an organ or tissue by which factor?
questions.explanation: Dose equivalent is calculated by multiplying the absorbed dose of an organ or tissue by the radiation weighting factor (wR), also known as the quality factor. The wR is a dimensionless factor that accounts for differences in relative biological effectiveness (RBE) among radiation types. It is distinct from the tissue weighting factor (wT), which is used to calculate effective dose.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the units of dose equivalent?
questions.explanation: Dose equivalent is expressed in Sievert (Sv), the SI unit, or rem (the older conventional unit). Values in diagnostic medicine are typically low and are therefore expressed in millisieverts (mSv) or millirem (mrem). The conversion is 100 rem = 1 Sv. Gray and rad are units of absorbed dose, which does not account for radiation quality.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The radiation weighting factor (wR) for alpha particles is:
questions.explanation: Alpha particles carry a radiation weighting factor of 20, the highest of the common radiation types. This reflects their high LET and correspondingly high relative biological effectiveness compared to gamma rays, x-rays, and beta particles, all of which have a wR of 1. This high weighting factor is why alpha emitters pose substantial radiobiological risk when internalized, despite their short range in tissue.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following radiation types carries a weighting factor of 10?
questions.explanation: Fast neutrons have a radiation weighting factor of 10. Slow neutrons have a lower weighting factor of 5, reflecting their reduced biological effectiveness relative to fast neutrons. Alpha particles have the highest weighting factor at 20, while beta particles, gamma rays, and x-rays all have a weighting factor of 1.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly lists these radiation types in order of increasing radiation weighting factor?

choices.text: X-rays -> fast neutrons -> slow neutrons -> alpha particles
Alpha particles -> fast neutrons -> slow neutrons -> x-rays
Slow neutrons -> x-rays -> fast neutrons -> alpha particles
X-rays -> slow neutrons -> fast neutrons -> alpha particles

questions.explanation: In order of increasing radiation weighting factor: x-rays (wR = 1), slow neutrons (wR = 5), fast neutrons (wR = 10), and alpha particles (wR = 20). Beta particles and gamma rays share the same weighting factor as x-rays (wR = 1). Higher weighting factors reflect greater relative biological effectiveness per unit of absorbed dose.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Effective dose is calculated by:

choices.text: Multiplying absorbed dose by a radiation weighting factor
Multiplying radioactivity by exposure time and tissue mass
Multiplying dose equivalent by a tissue weighting factor
Summing the deep-dose equivalent and shallow-dose equivalent

questions.explanation: Effective dose is the product of the organ or tissue dose equivalent (HT) and the tissue weighting factor (wT) for each organ or tissue irradiated, summed across all irradiated organs (HE = SUM of wT x HT). The tissue weighting factor accounts for the relative radiosensitivity of different organs to radiation-induced cancer. This is distinct from dose equivalent, which is calculated by multiplying absorbed dose by the radiation weighting factor.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly orders these organs from highest to lowest tissue weighting factor?
questions.explanation: From highest to lowest tissue weighting factor: lung (wT = 0.12, shared with colon, red bone marrow, stomach, and breast), gonads (wT = 0.08), thyroid (wT = 0.04, shared with bladder, liver, and esophagus), and skin (wT = 0.01, shared with bone surface, brain, and salivary glands). Organs with higher weighting factors are considered more sensitive to radiation-induced carcinogenesis.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following organs has the LOWEST tissue weighting factor?
questions.explanation: The brain has a tissue weighting factor of 0.01, placing it in the lowest tier alongside bone surface, salivary glands, and skin. The thyroid and liver each carry a weighting factor of 0.04, and the gonads carry 0.08. The lowest-weighted organs are considered less sensitive to radiation-induced carcinogenesis relative to organs like the lung, colon, red bone marrow, and stomach, which have the highest tissue weighting factor of 0.12.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Total Effective Dose Equivalent (TEDE) is defined as:

choices.text: The absorbed dose multiplied by the radiation weighting factor for all exposed organs
The dose equivalent to the whole body from background radiation sources only
The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the shallow-dose equivalent
The sum of the effective dose equivalent from external exposure and the committed effective dose equivalent from internal exposure

questions.explanation: TEDE is a dosimetry quantity defined by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) as the sum of the effective dose equivalent from external exposure and the committed effective dose equivalent from internal exposure (from inhaled or ingested radioactive material), thereby accounting for all known exposures. It is the comprehensive measure used to monitor and control total human exposure to ionizing radiation.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: On average, U.S. inhabitants receive approximately how much radiation dose per year from natural background radiation alone?
questions.explanation: The average U.S. inhabitant receives approximately 3.1 mSv per year from natural background radiation, most of which comes from radon in the air, with smaller contributions from cosmic rays and radiation from the earth itself. An additional 2.2 mSv per year comes from man-made sources, primarily medical procedures, bringing the total average annual dose from all sources to approximately 5.3 mSv.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Including both natural background and man-made sources, the total average annual radiation dose to a U.S. inhabitant is approximately:
questions.explanation: The total average annual dose is approximately 5.3 mSv, combining approximately 3.1 mSv from natural background radiation (primarily radon) and approximately 2.2 mSv from man-made sources (predominantly medical procedures). This level of yearly dose from all radiation sources has not been shown to cause harm in humans.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Below what effective dose threshold has radiation exposure not been shown to cause detectable harm in humans?
questions.explanation: Cancer risk from radiation exposure is too small to observe below 100 mSv. While the linear no-threshold (LNT) model assumes that any dose carries some theoretical risk, epidemiological evidence of actual harm is not detectable at doses below this level. This is relevant context when counseling patients about the risks of medical imaging procedures.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly identifies the three general categories of biological effects resulting from radiation exposure?
questions.explanation: The three general categories are genetic (hereditary) effects, which are passed on to the offspring of the exposed individual; somatic effects, which affect the cells and tissues of the exposed individual and are further subdivided into deterministic (tissue) and stochastic effects; and teratogenic effects, which refer to developmental abnormalities or birth defects resulting from in utero radiation exposure. Deterministic and stochastic are subcategories of somatic effects, not independent top-level categories.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Teratogenic effects of radiation refer to:

choices.text: Hereditary effects passed on to the offspring of the exposed individual
Stochastic effects that manifest years after exposure
Developmental abnormalities or birth defects occurring in a fetus due to in utero radiation exposure
Radiation effects on the cells and tissues of the exposed individual

questions.explanation: Teratogenic effects specifically refer to developmental abnormalities or birth defects that occur in a fetus as a result of in utero radiation exposure during pregnancy. They are distinct from genetic effects, which are heritable mutations passed on to future generations, and from somatic effects, which involve the exposed individual's own cells and tissues.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the direct pathway of radiation-induced cell injury?

choices.text: Radiation directly induces single- or double-stranded DNA breaks leading to cell death
Radiation depletes intracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) stores, causing metabolic failure
Radiation disrupts the cell membrane, causing osmotic imbalance and lysis
Radiation generates reactive oxygen species that damage proteins, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), and lipids

questions.explanation: In the direct pathway, radiation directly induces single-stranded (ssDNA) or double-stranded (dsDNA) DNA breaks that lead to cell death. Higher LET radiation leads to more double-stranded breaks, which are more difficult for the cell to repair accurately. DNA damage through the direct pathway is particularly problematic during phases of the cell cycle when repair mechanisms are not active.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the indirect pathway of radiation-induced cell injury?

choices.text: Radiation directly breaks chemical bonds within the deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) double helix
Radiation induces mitotic catastrophe by destabilizing the mitotic spindle
Radiation generates reactive oxygen species that damage proteins, DNA, and lipids
Radiation causes loss of membrane integrity through direct lipid peroxidation

questions.explanation: In the indirect pathway, radiation interacts with water molecules to generate reactive oxygen species (free radicals), which then damage proteins, DNA, and lipids, resulting in cell death. Because water is abundant in tissue, the indirect pathway accounts for a significant portion of radiation-induced cell injury. Cells in an oxygen-rich environment are particularly vulnerable to indirect effects because oxygen enhances free radical production.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Cells in an oxygen-rich environment are most at risk from which pathway of radiation injury?

choices.text: Both pathways equally, as oxygen amplifies all radiation effects
The direct pathway, due to enhanced deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) strand break frequency
The indirect pathway, due to greater production of reactive oxygen species

questions.explanation: Cells in an oxygen-rich environment are more at risk from the indirect pathway of radiation injury. Water serves as an abundant source of oxygen for this process, and increased oxygen availability promotes the formation of reactive oxygen species following radiation exposure, amplifying indirect cell damage. This oxygen enhancement effect is well recognized in radiation biology.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: During which phase of the cell cycle are cells MOST sensitive to radiation?
questions.explanation: Cells are most sensitive to radiation during the G2/M phase of the cell cycle, when deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) is compacted into tighter bundles and DNA repair mechanisms are not active. This makes DNA damage harder to repair accurately. Conversely, cells in late S phase are most radioresistant because active DNA replication is accompanied by robust DNA repair mechanisms.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: During which phase of the cell cycle are cells MOST radioresistant?
questions.explanation: Cells in late S phase are the most radioresistant because deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) repair mechanisms are most active during this phase of replication. This is in direct contrast to cells in G2/M phase, which are most radiosensitive due to condensed chromatin and inactive repair pathways.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following cell types is considered the most radiosensitive?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes (hematopoietic cells) are among the most radiosensitive cell types, along with spermatogonia cells and gastrointestinal stem cells. Radiosensitivity is associated with active cell division; these cells are rapidly proliferating and therefore more vulnerable to radiation damage. In contrast, nerve and muscle cells are among the most radioresistant because they are not actively dividing.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following cell types is considered most radioresistant?
questions.explanation: Nerve cells are among the most radioresistant cell types, along with muscle cells. Radioresistance is associated with a lack of active cell division. Hematopoietic cells (including lymphocytes and stem cells), spermatogonia, and gastrointestinal stem cells are actively proliferating and therefore among the most radiosensitive cell types.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Higher LET radiation leads to which of the following, compared to lower LET radiation?

choices.text: Preferential damage to the indirect pathway only
Fewer DNA breaks but greater membrane damage
More single-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) breaks only
More double-stranded DNA breaks and higher frequency of single-stranded breaks

questions.explanation: Higher LET radiation leads to more double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) breaks as well as a higher frequency of single-stranded breaks. Double-stranded breaks are particularly damaging because they are more difficult for cellular repair mechanisms to fix accurately, increasing the likelihood of cell death or mutation. This is one reason high-LET radiation (such as alpha particles) is more biologically effective per unit of absorbed dose.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The LD 50/30 is defined as:

choices.text: The dose expected to cause death in 50% of an exposed population within 30 days
The dose causing lethality in 30% of an exposed population within 50 days
The dose causing 50% lethality within 30 weeks in an exposed population
The dose at which 30% of cells survive after 50 Gy of exposure

questions.explanation: The LD 50/30 is the dose of radiation expected to cause death in 50% of an exposed population within 30 days. For humans, this value typically falls in the range of 400 to 450 rem (4 to 5 Sv) received over a very short period. This figure assumes no medical intervention; supportive care and intensive treatment can significantly increase survival at doses above this range.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The LD 50/30 for whole-body radiation exposure in humans is typically in the range of:
questions.explanation: The LD 50/30 for humans is typically in the range of 400 to 450 rem (4 to 5 Sv) received over a very short period, without medical intervention. Values below this range (100-300 rem) would not be expected to cause death in 50% of the population within 30 days, while values above (600-700 rem) would imply lethality in a far higher proportion of exposed individuals.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following best characterizes deterministic effects of radiation?

choices.text: No dose threshold exists; any exposure carries some risk
Effects are random and unrelated to dose magnitude
Severity increases with dose; a threshold must be exceeded before effects appear
Probability of occurrence increases with dose; severity is dose-independent

questions.explanation: Deterministic effects are defined by two key features: the severity of the effect increases with dose, and there is a threshold dose below which no effects are observed. These effects are typically seen soon after exposure once the threshold is exceeded. Common examples include skin erythema, epilation, and cataracts. This contrasts with stochastic effects, which have no threshold and for which the probability rather than the severity increases with dose.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: What is the approximate threshold dose for transient erythema and epilation following radiation exposure?
questions.explanation: Transient erythema and epilation (hair loss) have a threshold dose of approximately 2 Gy, with onset occurring within approximately 24 hours of exposure. Higher doses produce progressively more severe skin reactions: dry desquamation occurs at a threshold of 8 Gy with onset around 4 weeks, and moist desquamation requires approximately 15 Gy with a similar 4-week onset.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Dry desquamation following radiation exposure has a threshold dose of approximately 8 Gy. What is the typical time to onset?
questions.explanation: Dry desquamation has a threshold dose of approximately 8 Gy and typically appears around 4 weeks after exposure. This is in contrast to transient erythema and epilation, which occur at a lower threshold of 2 Gy and appear within about 24 hours. Moist desquamation, the more severe form, requires a threshold of approximately 15 Gy and also has an onset of approximately 4 weeks.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: What is the threshold dose for moist desquamation following radiation exposure?
questions.explanation: Moist desquamation has a threshold dose of approximately 15 Gy, with an onset of approximately 4 weeks. It represents a more severe skin reaction than dry desquamation (threshold 8 Gy) and transient erythema or epilation (threshold 2 Gy). All three skin reactions are deterministic effects, meaning their severity increases with dose above the relevant threshold.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The threshold dose for cataract formation following a single acute radiation exposure is:
questions.explanation: Cataract formation from a single acute radiation exposure has a threshold of 0.5 Gy. Lens opacification from a single acute exposure has a threshold range of 0.5-2 Gy, while fractionated exposure can cause opacification at as low as 0.5 Gy. These thresholds are considerably lower than those for skin reactions such as erythema (2 Gy), dry desquamation (8 Gy), and moist desquamation (15 Gy), highlighting the particular radiosensitivity of the lens.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Lens opacification from fractionated radiation exposure has a threshold of:
questions.explanation: The threshold for lens opacification from fractionated radiation exposure is 0.5 Gy. By comparison, a single acute exposure can cause opacification at a threshold range of 0.5-2 Gy, and cataract formation from a single acute exposure also carries a threshold of 0.5 Gy. The lens of the eye is notably radiosensitive, and opacification may have a delayed onset of years depending on dose and fractionation.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following best characterizes stochastic effects of radiation?

choices.text: Effects occur only above a defined threshold dose; severity increases with dose
Effects are reversible and typically appear within hours of exposure
Severity and probability both increase proportionally with dose
Probability of occurrence increases with dose; severity is independent of dose

questions.explanation: Stochastic effects are defined by the fact that the probability of occurrence increases with dose, but the severity of the effect does not depend on the dose. A person who develops radiation-induced cancer after a high dose does not necessarily have a more severe cancer than someone who develops it after a lower dose. There is no threshold for stochastic effects, a principle formalized in the linear no-threshold (LNT) model.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The linear no-threshold (LNT) model applies to which category of radiation effects?
questions.explanation: The linear no-threshold model applies to stochastic effects. It holds that the probability of a stochastic effect (primarily carcinogenesis or genetic mutation) increases linearly with dose, with no threshold below which the risk is zero. This is a conservative approach to radiation protection. Deterministic effects, by contrast, do have a threshold and are not governed by the LNT model.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following are the primary types of stochastic radiation effects?

choices.text: Teratogenic defects and somatic cell death

questions.explanation: The primary types of stochastic effects are carcinogenesis (radiation-induced cancer) and genetic effects (heritable mutations). These occur probabilistically with no dose threshold, and their severity does not depend on dose magnitude. Skin erythema, epilation, cataracts, and desquamation are all deterministic effects with defined thresholds, not stochastic effects.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the linear no-threshold (LNT) model is correct?

choices.text: It applies primarily to deterministic effects such as cataracts and skin burns
It establishes that severity of effects increases proportionally with dose at all dose levels
It assumes that any radiation dose, however small, carries some probability of causing a stochastic effect
It predicts that effects only occur above a minimum threshold dose

questions.explanation: The LNT model assumes that any radiation dose, no matter how small, carries some nonzero probability of causing a stochastic harm such as cancer or heritable mutation. This is a conservative approach that provides a practical basis for radiation protection policy. It stands in contrast to deterministic effects, which require a threshold dose to be exceeded before any effect is observed.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: A radiation worker receives a single acute whole-body exposure of 3 Gy. Which of the following deterministic effects would be expected at this dose?

choices.text: No deterministic effects; the dose falls below all established thresholds

questions.explanation: Transient erythema and epilation have a threshold of 2 Gy, so a 3 Gy exposure exceeds this threshold and these effects would be expected, with onset within approximately 24 hours. Dry desquamation requires a threshold of 8 Gy, and moist desquamation requires 15 Gy - both well above the dose received. Lens opacification (threshold 0.5-2 Gy) would also be expected at 3 Gy, but is not among the choices. The key principle here is that only deterministic effects with thresholds at or below the actual dose will manifest.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: An individual receives a single acute whole-body radiation exposure of 12 Gy. Which of the following effects would NOT be expected at this dose?
questions.explanation: At 12 Gy, the thresholds for transient erythema and epilation (2 Gy), lens opacification (0.5-2 Gy), and dry desquamation (8 Gy) have all been exceeded, so these effects would be expected. Moist desquamation, however, has a threshold of 15 Gy - which a 12 Gy exposure does not reach. This question illustrates the importance of knowing not just individual thresholds but understanding which effects "stack" as dose increases above successive thresholds.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Following a single acute radiation exposure, a patient develops only lens opacification with no skin findings. Which of the following dose ranges is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Lens opacification from a single acute exposure has a threshold of 0.5 Gy, while transient erythema and epilation do not appear until 2 Gy. A dose between 0.5 Gy and just under 2 Gy would therefore be above the opacification threshold but below the threshold for cutaneous effects, consistent with isolated lens findings. Below 0.5 Gy, no deterministic effects would be expected. At 2 Gy or above, skin findings such as erythema and epilation would also be expected alongside the lens changes.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: How many mrem are equivalent to 1 mSv?
questions.explanation: 100 mrem is equivalent to 1 mSv. This conversion applies across the dose equivalent and effective dose frameworks - rem and Sievert are the base units, and their milli- prefixed forms follow the same ratio (100 rem = 1 Sv). Familiarity with this conversion is essential for translating between the conventional unit system (rem/mrem) used in much of U.S. regulatory practice and the SI unit system (Sv/mSv) used in international and clinical contexts.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: "Collective dose" is defined as:

choices.text: The sum of individual doses received by a specified population from a specified source over a given period
The total lifetime radiation dose received by a single individual
The combined external and internal dose equivalent for a radiation worker
The average annual dose to all radiation workers at a given facility

questions.explanation: Collective dose is the sum of the individual doses received in a given period by a specified population from exposure to a specified source of radiation. It is a population-level dosimetry concept, distinct from individual dose metrics such as total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) or effective dose equivalent, which describe exposure to a single person.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The largest single contributor to natural background radiation exposure in the U.S. is:
questions.explanation: Radon in the air accounts for the largest portion of natural background radiation, comprising approximately 68% of ubiquitous background exposure. Cosmic rays (space) contribute approximately 11%, terrestrial radiation approximately 7%, and Radon-220, Potassium-40, and the thorium and uranium series each contribute smaller fractions. This is why radon exposure in homes and buildings is a significant public health concern.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly orders these sources of natural background radiation from highest to lowest contribution?
questions.explanation: From highest to lowest contribution to natural background radiation: Radon-222 (approximately 68%), cosmic rays/space (approximately 11%), terrestrial radiation (approximately 7%), and Radon-220 (approximately 5%). Potassium-40 and the thorium and uranium series each contribute approximately 4-5%, placing them in the same tier as Radon-220. Radon-222 dominates background exposure by a wide margin.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which imaging modality contributes the largest share of collective medical radiation exposure to the U.S. population?
questions.explanation: Computed tomography accounts for approximately 62% of collective medical radiation exposure in the United States, by far the largest share of any imaging modality. Nuclear medicine is second at approximately 18%, followed by radiography and fluoroscopy at 9%, cardiac interventional fluoroscopy at 6%, and noncardiac interventional fluoroscopy at 5%.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: After computed tomography, which imaging modality contributes the second largest share of collective medical radiation exposure?
questions.explanation: Nuclear medicine accounts for approximately 18% of collective medical radiation exposure, making it the second largest contributor after computed tomography (62%). Radiography and fluoroscopy contribute approximately 9%, cardiac interventional fluoroscopy 6%, and noncardiac interventional fluoroscopy 5%.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The average effective dose from a body computed tomography (CT) is approximately:
questions.explanation: The average effective dose from a body CT is approximately 6 mSv. By comparison, a head CT delivers approximately 1.5 mSv, natural background radiation accounts for approximately 3 mSv per year, and living in Denver, Colorado - a higher-altitude city with increased cosmic ray exposure - is associated with approximately 10 mSv per year. The body CT dose of 6 mSv is well below the 100 mSv threshold below which cancer risk is too small to observe.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The average effective dose from a head computed tomography (CT) is approximately:
questions.explanation: The average effective dose from a head CT is approximately 1.5 mSv. This is notably less than a body CT (approximately 6 mSv), reflecting the smaller tissue volume irradiated and the absence of highly radiosensitive abdominal organs. An abdominopelvic x-ray delivers approximately 0.6 mSv, and natural background radiation accounts for approximately 3 mSv per year.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The average effective dose from an adult chest x-ray is approximately:
questions.explanation: The average effective dose from an adult chest x-ray is approximately 0.1 mSv. A pediatric chest x-ray delivers approximately one-tenth of that, at 0.01 mSv. A mammogram delivers approximately 0.4 mSv, and an abdominopelvic x-ray approximately 0.6 mSv. These differences reflect both the radiation technique used and the relative radiosensitivity of the tissues in the field of view.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: The average effective dose from a pediatric chest x-ray is approximately:
questions.explanation: The average effective dose from a pediatric chest x-ray is approximately 0.01 mSv, which is one-tenth the dose of an adult chest x-ray (0.1 mSv). An extremity x-ray delivers even less, approximately 0.001 mSv, while a mammogram delivers approximately 0.4 mSv. The lower dose in pediatric chest imaging reflects smaller patient size and optimized exposure parameters.

questions.chapterName: Section 2: Radiation Biology
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly orders these imaging studies from lowest to highest average effective dose?

choices.text: Mammogram -> adult chest x-ray -> abdominopelvic x-ray -> body CT
Adult chest x-ray -> mammogram -> body CT -> head CT
Mammogram -> abdominopelvic x-ray -> head computed tomography (CT) -> body CT
Adult chest x-ray -> abdominopelvic x-ray -> mammogram -> head CT

questions.explanation: From lowest to highest average effective dose: mammogram (approximately 0.4 mSv), abdominopelvic x-ray (approximately 0.6 mSv), head CT (approximately 1.5 mSv), and body CT (approximately 6 mSv). Option B incorrectly places body CT above head CT. Option C incorrectly places abdominopelvic x-ray above mammogram. Option D incorrectly places mammogram below adult chest x-ray (mammogram is 0.4 mSv; adult chest x-ray is 0.1 mSv).

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Regulatory authority over radioactive material shipments in the United States is shared between which two agencies?

choices.text: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
The FDA and the Department of Transportation
The NRC and the Department of Homeland Security
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and the Department of Transportation

questions.explanation: The safety of radioactive material shipments is the joint responsibility of the NRC and the Department of Transportation (DOT). The NRC establishes requirements for the design and manufacture of packages, while the DOT regulates shipments while they are in transit and sets standards for labeling and smaller quantity packages.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Type A and Type B radioactive material packages differ primarily in which of the following ways?

choices.text: Type A packages are designed to survive normal handling and minor accidents; Type B to survive severe accidents
Type A packages are used for liquid materials only; Type B for solid materials
Type A packages require a transport index; Type B do not
Type A packages are used for therapeutic quantities; Type B for diagnostic quantities

questions.explanation: Type A packages are designed to survive normal transportation handling and minor accidents, and most radioactive materials in clinical use are transported in Type A packages. Type B packaging is designed to withstand severe accidents. Both types must be certified by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), which requires demonstration through actual testing or computer analysis that the package can withstand a series of accident conditions.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The type of label required on a radioactive material package is determined by:

choices.text: The physical half-life of the radionuclide being shipped
The radiation levels measured at the package surface and at 1 meter from the package
Whether the package is classified as Type A or Type B
The total activity of the radioactive material contained inside the package

questions.explanation: Although the type of package required for transport is based on the activity inside the package, the label required on the package is based on the radiation hazard outside the package, specifically the radiation levels at the surface and at 1 meter. This distinction is important: the same radionuclide at different shielding levels could require different labels even if the internal activity is identical.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The transport index (TI) on a radioactive material package represents:

choices.text: The surface radiation level at the point of highest exposure, expressed in mrem/hr
The ratio of internal activity to external dose rate
The highest radiation level at 1 meter from the surface of the package, expressed in mrem/hr
The total activity inside the package expressed in millicuries

questions.explanation: The transport index is the highest radiation level at 1 meter from the surface of the package, expressed in mrem/hr. It is written on the package label and is used by carriers to manage cumulative radiation exposure during transport. Only the White I label does not carry a transport index.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which radioactive material package label does NOT require a transport index?

choices.text: All labels require a transport index

questions.explanation: The White I label is the only radioactive material label that does not require a transport index. Yellow II and Yellow III labels both require a transport index because the radiation levels at 1 meter are high enough to be relevant to carrier safety. The White I label is used for packages with very low external radiation levels (at or below 0.5 mrem/hr at both the surface and at 1 meter).

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: What is the maximum allowable surface radiation level for a package that may be labeled White I?
questions.explanation: A White I label requires that the surface radiation level be at or below 0.5 mrem/hr, and the radiation level at 1 meter must also be at or below 0.5 mrem/hr. This is the most restrictive label category. A Yellow II label applies when the surface level exceeds 0.5 mrem/hr but remains at or below 50 mrem/hr.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: What is the maximum allowable surface radiation level for a package bearing a Yellow II label?
questions.explanation: A Yellow II label is required when the surface radiation level exceeds 0.5 mrem/hr but remains at or below 50 mrem/hr, and the radiation level at 1 meter is at or below 1 mrem/hr. When the surface level exceeds 50 mrem/hr, a Yellow III label is required instead.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: What is the maximum transport index permitted for a Yellow II labeled package?
questions.explanation: A Yellow II label requires a transport index of no greater than 1, reflecting a radiation level at 1 meter of no more than 1 mrem/hr. A Yellow III label is required when the transport index exceeds 1, up to a maximum of 10. The transport index is written on the label and allows carriers to track cumulative exposure across multiple packages.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: What is the maximum allowable surface radiation level for a package bearing a Yellow III label?
questions.explanation: A Yellow III label applies when the surface radiation level exceeds 50 mrem/hr and is at or below 200 mrem/hr, or when the radiation level at 1 meter exceeds 1 mrem/hr and is at or below 10 mrem/hr. Surface levels above 200 mrem/hr are not permitted for standard transport labels.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: What is the maximum transport index permitted for a Yellow III labeled package?
questions.explanation: A Yellow III label requires a transport index greater than 1 but no more than 10. A Yellow II transport index (TI) is capped at 1. A TI greater than 10 is only permissible under specific exclusive use transport conditions, not under standard labeled package transport.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: What is the maximum transport index permitted for packages transported in nonexclusive use (common carrier) vehicles?
questions.explanation: The maximum transport index for nonexclusive use (common carrier) vehicles is 10. The same limit of 10 applies to exclusive use open vehicles. Only exclusive use closed vehicles (contract carriers) may carry packages with a transport index exceeding 10, where the radiation level at 1 meter from the package surface may exceed 10 mrem/hr.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Under which of the following conditions may the radiation level at 1 meter from a radioactive material package exceed 10 mrem/hr during transport?

choices.text: Any common carrier vehicle with a trained radiation worker as the driver
Any exclusive use vehicle, open or closed
An exclusive use open vehicle with appropriate placarding
An exclusive use closed vehicle (contract carrier)

questions.explanation: The radiation level at 1 meter from the surface of a package may exceed 10 mrem/hr only if the package is transported in an exclusive use (contract carrier) closed vehicle. Both common carriers and exclusive use open vehicles are subject to a maximum transport index of 10. The closed vehicle provides additional shielding and restricts access to the cargo area.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT required to appear on a radioactive material container label?
questions.explanation: Required label information includes the radionuclide(s) present, quantity of radioactivity, radioactivity date, radiation levels, kinds of materials, and mass enrichment. Manufacturer name and address is not among the required label elements. This label information allows carriers and recipients to identify the contents and associated hazard without opening the package.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Before an empty, uncontaminated radioactive material container may be removed to an unrestricted area, the licensee must:

choices.text: Obtain written authorization from the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)
Remove or deface the radioactive material label, or clearly indicate the container no longer contains radioactive material
Perform a wipe test confirming activity below 185 Bq
Store the container for at least 10 half-lives before disposal

questions.explanation: Prior to removal or disposal of empty, uncontaminated containers to unrestricted areas, the licensee must remove or deface the radioactive material label, or otherwise clearly indicate that the container no longer contains radioactive material. This prevents confusion and protects the public from unnecessary concern about containers that no longer pose a radiation hazard.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: When a labeled radioactive material package is received during normal working hours, it must be monitored for contamination and radiation levels within:
questions.explanation: Monitoring must be performed as soon as practical after receipt, but no later than 3 hours after the package is received at the licensee's facility during normal working hours. If the package is received after working hours, monitoring must be completed within 3 hours from the beginning of the next working day. Monitoring includes checking with a Geiger-Mueller detector for radioactive contamination and radiation levels, and assessing for physical evidence of package degradation.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: A labeled radioactive material package is delivered to a nuclear medicine facility at 6:00 PM, after normal working hours. By what time must it be monitored?

choices.text: At any time on the next working day
Within 3 hours of receipt, regardless of time of day
Within 3 hours of the start of the next working day
Within 8 hours of the start of the next working day

questions.explanation: If a labeled package is received after normal working hours, monitoring must be completed no later than 3 hours from the beginning of the next working day. This is distinct from the rule for packages received during working hours, which requires monitoring within 3 hours of receipt. The 3-hour window from the start of the next working day provides a consistent, enforceable deadline regardless of exactly when after-hours delivery occurred.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Upon receipt of a labeled radioactive material shipment, which of the following agents would be exempt from external surface contamination monitoring?
questions.explanation: Licensees are required to monitor the external surfaces of labeled packages for radioactive contamination, unless the package contains only radioactive material in the form of a gas or is designated as an excepted package. Xenon-133, being a gas, falls under this exemption. Technetium-99m, thallium-201, and iodine-123 are all non-gaseous radiopharmaceuticals and are not exempt from surface contamination monitoring.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: If surface contamination or external radiation levels on a received package exceed allowable limits, the licensee must immediately notify:

choices.text: The authorized user and the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)
The NRC Regional Office and the sending facility
The final delivery carrier and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Headquarters Operations Center

questions.explanation: If removable radioactive surface contamination or external radiation levels exceed the allowable limits, the licensee must immediately notify the final delivery carrier and the NRC Headquarters Operations Center by telephone. This prompt dual notification ensures both the transport chain and the regulatory authority are aware of the event so that appropriate protective actions can be taken.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Licensees who transfer special form sources in licensee-owned vehicles to and from a work site are exempt from which of the following requirements?

choices.text: Notifying the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) before transport
Surface contamination monitoring of the package
Radiation level surveys of the package

questions.explanation: Licensees transferring special form sources in licensee-owned or licensee-operated vehicles are exempt from the contamination monitoring requirement but are NOT exempt from the survey requirement for measuring radiation levels. The radiation level survey is still required to ensure the source remains properly lodged in its shielding.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Sealed sources must undergo leak testing at intervals not to exceed:
questions.explanation: Each sealed source must undergo leak tests (wipe tests) at intervals not exceeding 6 months. If a sealed source is transferred and the recipient does not have a certificate confirming that a leak test was performed within the prior 6 months, the source may not be used until it has been tested. This regular testing ensures that the sealed encapsulation remains intact and that radioactive material is not leaking into the environment.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: A required leak test reveals removable contamination on a sealed source. At what minimum activity level must this finding be reported?
questions.explanation: A licensee must file a report if a required leak test reveals the presence of 185 Bq (0.005 uCi) or more of removable contamination. This threshold is designed to detect meaningful leakage while avoiding reporting of trivial background-level findings. The report must be filed with the appropriate Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Regional Office with a copy to the Director of the Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: After discovering that a sealed source has leaked above the reportable threshold, within how many days must the licensee file a written report?
questions.explanation: A licensee must file a written report within 5 days of a required leak test revealing the presence of 185 Bq (0.005 uCi) or more of removable contamination. The report must include the model and serial number of the source, the radionuclide and its estimated activity, the results of the test, the date of the wipe test, and the corrective action taken.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT required to be included in a written report of a leaking sealed source?

choices.text: Date of the wipe test and corrective action taken
Names of all personnel present during the wipe test
Model number and serial number of the source

questions.explanation: The required contents of a leaked sealed source report include the model and serial number, the radionuclide and its estimated activity, the results of the test, the date of the wipe test, and the corrective action taken. The names of personnel present during the test are not a required element of the report, though the name of the person who performed the test may be retained in facility records.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: An authorized user of a diagnostic sealed source or authorized device must meet which of the following minimum training requirements?

choices.text: 60 hours of training including 8 hours of classroom and laboratory training
Specialty board certification recognized by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) or Agreement State (AS), or completion of 8 hours of classroom and laboratory training
Completion of an NRC-approved residency program in nuclear medicine
700 hours of training including 200 hours of classroom training

questions.explanation: To use a diagnostic sealed source or authorized device, the authorized user must be a physician, dentist, or podiatrist who is either certified by a specialty board recognized by the NRC or AS, or has completed at least 8 hours of classroom and laboratory training in basic radionuclide handling techniques specifically applicable to the device. The training must cover radiation physics, instrumentation, radiation protection, mathematics of radioactivity measurement, and radiation biology.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The radioactive material used in most household smoke detectors is:
questions.explanation: Smoke detectors contain tiny foils coated with americium-241 (Am-241), which provides a steady source of ions in the detector's analytical chamber. Gas and aerosol detector products such as smoke detectors are among the categories of exempt quantities of byproduct material. Nickel-63 (Ni-63) is used in chemical agent detectors, tritium is used in self-luminous products such as exit signs and gunsights, and carbon-14 is used in urea breath test capsules.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Capsules containing carbon-14 urea for in vivo diagnostic use are classified as an exempt quantity. What is the activity per capsule?
questions.explanation: Capsules containing 1 uCi of carbon-14 urea each, for in vivo diagnostic use in humans, are classified as an exempt quantity of byproduct material. This low activity allows these capsules to be used for the urea breath test without requiring a specific radioactive materials license for their possession.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an exempt quantity of byproduct material?

choices.text: Capsules containing 1 uCi of carbon-14 urea for diagnostic use

questions.explanation: Technetium-99m prepared for patient injection is a licensed radiopharmaceutical requiring full regulatory compliance and is not an exempt quantity. Exempt quantities include self-luminous products containing tritium (exit signs, gunsights), gas detector products containing Am-241 or Ni-63 (smoke detectors), and carbon-14 urea capsules at 1 uCi each for in vivo diagnostic use. Exempt quantities are those whose possession and use do not require a specific radioactive materials license.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Records of surveys, calibrations, and sealed source leak checks must be retained for how long?

choices.text: For the duration of the license

questions.explanation: Records showing the results of surveys, calibrations, and sealed source leak checks must be retained for 3 years after the record is made. This 3-year retention period applies to many operational records in nuclear medicine. Certain other records, such as those used to assess individual internal dose and environmental effluent monitoring, must be retained for the duration of the license.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following categories of records must be retained for the duration of the license, rather than the standard 3-year period?

choices.text: Results of surveys used to assess individual dose from external sources
Records of sealed source leak tests
Results of area radiation surveys performed at the end of each day

questions.explanation: Results of surveys used to determine the dose from external sources, when used in the assessment of individual dose equivalents, must be retained for the duration of the license. The same applies to results of measurements used to assess individual intakes of radioactive material, air sampling, bioassays, and effluent monitoring. In contrast, records of sealed source leak tests, instrument calibrations, and daily area surveys are retained for 3 years.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: How frequently must a licensee perform radiation surveys of areas where radioactive materials are used?

choices.text: At the beginning of each day of use
At the end of each day of use

questions.explanation: The licensee must survey with a Geiger-Mueller meter at the end of each day of use. Surveys must also be performed in all areas where unsealed byproduct material requiring a written directive was prepared or administered. Records of each survey must be retained for 3 years.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT required to be included in the record of an area radiation survey?

choices.text: The prescribed radiopharmaceutical dose administered that day
The instrument used to perform the survey
The name of the person who performed the survey

questions.explanation: Required elements of an area survey record include the survey date, the results of the survey, the instrument used, and the name of the person who performed it. The prescribed radiopharmaceutical dose is not a required component of the survey record; that information belongs in dosage records. This distinction reflects the different purposes of survey records (environmental monitoring) and dosage records (patient administration tracking).

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following is an acceptable method for disposing of licensed radioactive material?

choices.text: Transfer to any hospital waste contractor
Release into the sanitary sewer without restriction if the half-life is less than 120 days
Incineration by the licensee, provided the total activity is below 1 mCi
Transfer to an authorized recipient, decay in storage, or release in effluents within authorized limits

questions.explanation: Licensed material may only be disposed of by transfer to an authorized recipient, by decay in storage, or by release in effluents within authorized limits. Sewer release is subject to strict concentration and annual quantity limits, not simply half-life criteria. A person must be specifically licensed to receive waste for incineration or other treatment from other persons.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: For a licensee to discharge licensed radioactive material into the sanitary sewer system, the material must first meet which of the following conditions?

choices.text: The material must have a physical half-life of less than 120 days
The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) must approve each individual sewer release in writing
The material must be readily soluble or readily dispersible biological material in water
The total activity must not exceed 1 mCi per disposal event

questions.explanation: For sewer disposal, the material must be readily soluble (or readily dispersible biological material) in water, and the concentration released must not exceed predefined limits. Annual total quantity limits also apply. The half-life criterion applies to decay-in-storage, not sewer disposal. There is no requirement for RSO written approval of each individual sewer release.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: What is the maximum annual quantity of hydrogen-3 (tritium) a licensee may release into the sanitary sewer system?
questions.explanation: The annual sewer disposal limit for hydrogen-3 (tritium) is 5 curies (185 GBq). This limit is higher than for other radionuclides because tritium has a low energy beta emission and relatively low radiotoxicity. The limit for carbon-14 is 1 curie per year, and the limit for all other radioactive materials combined is also 1 curie per year.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: What is the maximum annual quantity of carbon-14 a licensee may release into the sanitary sewer system?
questions.explanation: The annual sewer disposal limit for carbon-14 is 1 curie (37 GBq).
