This is the same annual limit that applies to all other radioactive materials combined (excluding hydrogen-3, which has a higher limit of 5 Ci/year due to its lower radiotoxicity). These limits apply to the total released by the licensee over the calendar year.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: For all radioactive materials other than hydrogen-3 and carbon-14, what is the combined annual sewer disposal limit?
questions.explanation: The total annual sewer disposal limit for all radioactive materials other than hydrogen-3 and carbon-14, combined, is 1 curie (37 GBq). The three sewer limits to remember are: hydrogen-3 at 5 Ci/year, carbon-14 at 1 Ci/year, and all other radioactive materials combined at 1 Ci/year.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Patient excreta following administration of radioactive material for diagnosis or therapy:

choices.text: May only be released to the sewer if the administered activity was below 30 mCi
Must be collected and stored until activity decays below background
Are subject to the same sewer disposal concentration limits as other radioactive waste
Are not subject to the sewer disposal limitations that apply to other licensed materials

questions.explanation: Patient excreta from individuals undergoing medical diagnosis or therapy with radioactive material are explicitly exempt from the sewer disposal concentration and quantity limitations that apply to other licensed radioactive materials. This exemption recognizes the clinical reality that it is neither practical nor necessary to collect and hold patient urine and feces after radiopharmaceutical administration.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: For decay-in-storage to be used as a disposal method, the byproduct material must have a physical half-life of no more than:
questions.explanation: A licensee may hold byproduct material with a physical half-life of less than or equal to 120 days for decay-in-storage before disposal without regard to its radioactivity, provided that the activity is confirmed to be indistinguishable from background before release and all radiation labels are removed or obliterated prior to disposal.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Before releasing byproduct material held for decay-in-storage into the regular waste stream, the licensee must confirm which of the following?

choices.text: The elapsed time is at least 10 half-lives of the radionuclide
The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) has performed a final audit and signed off on the disposal
A survey with a Geiger-Mueller (GM) meter at the container surface shows activity indistinguishable from background, and all radiation labels have been removed
The material has been held for at least 6 months regardless of half-life

questions.explanation: Before disposing of decay-in-storage material, the licensee must monitor the byproduct material with a Geiger-Mueller meter at the surface and confirm that its radioactivity cannot be distinguished from background radiation on the most sensitive scale with no interposed shielding. All radiation labels must also be removed or obliterated prior to disposal, so the containers are not misidentified as radioactive waste.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Records of the disposal of licensed radioactive materials must be retained for how long?

choices.text: For the duration of the license

questions.explanation: Disposal records must be maintained for 3 years. This is consistent with the standard retention period for most operational records in nuclear medicine, including area survey records, calibration records, and sealed source leak test records.

questions.chapterName: Section 3: Transport and Management of Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT required to be included in the record of licensed radioactive material disposal?

choices.text: The total activity of material administered to patients that day
The radiation level measured at the surface of each waste container
The background radiation level at the time of disposal

questions.explanation: Required elements of a disposal record include the date of disposal, the survey instrument used, the background radiation level, the radiation level measured at the surface of each waste container, and the name of the individual who performed the survey. Total administered patient activity is tracked in dosage records, not disposal records. The disposal record focuses on confirming the waste is safe for release, not on tracking what was given to patients.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual occupational whole-body dose limit for an adult radiation worker is:
questions.explanation: The annual whole-body occupational dose limit for adult radiation workers is 5 rem. This is distinct from the limits for individual organs and skin/extremities (50 rem each) and the eye lens (15 rem). The 0.5 rem value applies to the whole-body limit for minors, not adults. If an adult worker exceeds 5 rem in less than a calendar year, they are not permitted in the radiation zone until the next calendar year.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual occupational dose limit for an individual organ in an adult radiation worker is:
questions.explanation: The annual occupational dose limit for an individual organ in an adult is 50 rem. This same limit applies to the skin and extremities. The whole-body limit for adults is 5 rem, and the eye lens limit is 15 rem. The minor organ limit is 5 rem, which is one-tenth of the adult organ limit.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual occupational dose limit for the skin or extremities (distal to the knee or elbow) in an adult radiation worker is:
questions.explanation: The annual occupational dose limit for the skin or extremities in adults is 50 rem, the same as the limit for individual organs. The eye lens carries a lower limit of 15 rem, the whole body is limited to 5 rem, and the minor equivalent for skin/extremities is 5 rem. The extremity limit applies specifically to areas distal to the knee or elbow.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual occupational dose limit for the eye lens in an adult radiation worker is:
questions.explanation: The annual occupational dose limit for the eye lens in adults is 15 rem. This is intermediate between the whole-body limit (5 rem) and the organ/skin/extremity limit (50 rem), reflecting the particular radiosensitivity of the lens and the risk of radiation-induced cataract formation. The minor eye lens limit is 1.5 rem, which is 10% of the adult value.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual occupational whole-body dose limit for a minor (under 18 years) working in a radiation environment is:
questions.explanation: The annual whole-body dose limit for minors is 0.5 rem, which is 10% of the adult whole-body limit of 5 rem. The minor eye lens limit is 1.5 rem, and the minor organ and skin/extremity limits are each 5 rem. The value 0.1 rem is the annual dose limit for members of the public.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual occupational dose limit for an individual organ in a minor (under 18 years) is:
questions.explanation: The annual occupational dose limit for an individual organ in a minor is 5 rem, which is 10% of the adult organ limit of 50 rem. The minor whole-body limit is 0.5 rem, the eye lens limit is 1.5 rem, and the skin/extremity limit is also 5 rem. The value 15 rem is the adult eye lens limit.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual occupational dose limit for the skin or extremities in a minor (under 18 years) is:
questions.explanation: The annual occupational dose limit for the skin or extremities in a minor is 5 rem, equal to 10% of the adult limit of 50 rem. This value is shared with the minor individual organ limit. The minor whole-body limit is 0.5 rem and the eye lens limit is 1.5 rem. The value 50 rem is the adult skin/extremity limit.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual occupational dose limit for the eye lens in a minor (under 18 years) is:
questions.explanation: The annual occupational eye lens dose limit for minors is 1.5 rem, which is 10% of the adult eye lens limit of 15 rem. The minor whole-body limit is 0.5 rem, and the organ and skin/extremity limits are each 5 rem. The 15 rem value is the adult, not the minor, eye lens limit.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual occupational dose limits for minors represent what percentage of the corresponding adult dose limits?
questions.explanation: The annual occupational dose limits for minors are 10% of the adult limits across all categories. This applies uniformly: whole body (adult 5 rem, minor 0.5 rem), individual organ (adult 50 rem, minor 5 rem), skin/extremities (adult 50 rem, minor 5 rem), and eye lens (adult 15 rem, minor 1.5 rem). This protective reduction reflects the greater radiosensitivity of developing tissues in individuals under 18.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: An adult radiation worker exceeds the 5 rem whole-body dose limit partway through the calendar year. Which of the following best describes the regulatory consequence?

choices.text: A mandatory written report must be filed with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) within 30 days
The excess dose is subtracted from the next quarter's monitoring allowance
The worker must undergo a mandatory medical evaluation before returning to work
The worker may not enter the radiation zone until the following calendar year

questions.explanation: If an adult radiation worker exceeds the 5 rem whole-body dose limit in less than a year, whether employed at one or multiple places, the individual will not be allowed in the radiation zone until the next calendar year. Additionally, doses received in excess of annual limits, including those from accidents or emergencies, must be subtracted from the limits for planned special exposures in the current year and over the individual's lifetime.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The dose limit for the embryo/fetus of a declared pregnant radiation worker is:
questions.explanation: The dose limit for the embryo/fetus of a declared pregnant radiation worker is 0.5 rem. This is the same numerical value as the annual whole-body limit for minors, but it applies to the entire gestation period rather than a calendar year. The public limit of 0.1 rem per year and the 0.05 rem compliance buffer for late-declared pregnancies are related but distinct values.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The 0.5 rem dose limit for the embryo/fetus of a declared pregnant worker applies over which time period?
questions.explanation: The 0.5 rem embryo/fetus dose limit applies to the entire gestation period, not per month, trimester, or year. This is an important distinction from the public limit (0.1 rem per year) and the minor limit (0.5 rem per year). The entire-gestation timeframe means the cumulative dose from the moment of declaration through delivery must remain below this threshold.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The annual dose limit to individual members of the public from a licensed operation is:
questions.explanation: The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from a licensed operation must not exceed 0.1 rem (100 mrem) per year. This limit excludes background radiation, any radioactive material administered directly to the individual, exposure from individuals who have received radioactive material, and voluntary participation in medical research. The 0.5 rem value is the dose limit for the embryo/fetus and for visitors or caregivers of hospitalized radioactive patients.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The 0.1 rem dose limit for members of the public from a licensed operation applies over which time period?

choices.text: Per visit to a licensed facility
For any continuous period of exposure

questions.explanation: The 0.1 rem public dose limit applies per calendar year. This is in contrast to the embryo/fetus limit (0.5 rem over the entire gestation) and the visitor/caregiver limit (0.5 rem for the duration of contact). The annual nature of the public limit means cumulative exposure from all licensed operations must be tracked over the year.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The radiation dose limit for a visitor or caregiver of a hospitalized individual receiving radioactive material is:
questions.explanation: The dose limit for a visitor or caregiver/family member is 0.5 rem. This is the same numerical value as the embryo/fetus dose limit, but differs in its time frame. The 0.1 rem value is the annual public dose limit; when a licensee wishes to allow a visitor to receive more than 0.1 rem but less than 0.5 rem, the authorized user must determine before the visit that it is appropriate.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The 0.5 rem dose limit for a visitor or caregiver of a hospitalized radioactive patient applies over which time period?

choices.text: For the duration of contact with the patient

questions.explanation: The 0.5 rem limit for visitors and caregivers applies for the duration of contact, not per visit or per year. This framing accommodates the variable and ongoing nature of caregiving relationships during a patient's radioactive treatment period, and it is intentionally different from the 0.1 rem annual public limit.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Under Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) regulations, which of the following individuals is NOT considered a member of the public?

choices.text: A family member visiting a hospitalized radioactive patient
A patient who has received a therapeutic radiopharmaceutical
A caregiver assisting a patient at home following radioiodine therapy
A hospital employee working in administration

questions.explanation: A patient is explicitly not considered a member of the public under NRC regulations. This distinction matters because the 0.1 rem annual public dose limit does not apply to doses received by the patient themselves. Family members, visitors, caregivers, and non-radiation hospital staff are all subject to public or visitor dose limits, but the patient is not.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: A licensee wishes to allow a visitor to spend time with an inpatient who has received radioiodine therapy. The projected dose to the visitor is 0.3 rem. Which of the following is required before the visit may proceed?

choices.text: The visit is not permitted because it exceeds the 0.1 rem public dose limit
The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) must be present during the visit to monitor exposure
Written informed consent from the visitor is required by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
The authorized user must determine before the visit that it is appropriate

questions.explanation: A licensee may permit visitors to an individual who cannot be released to receive more than 0.1 rem, provided the dose does not exceed 0.5 rem and the authorized user has determined before the visit that it is appropriate. The Authorized User (AU)'s prospective approval is the key regulatory requirement here. Neither RSO presence nor visitor written consent is required by regulation.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT excluded from the calculation of the 0.1 rem annual public dose limit?

choices.text: Exposure from being near individuals who have received radioactive material
Radioactive material the individual themselves received as a patient
Radiation received while working as a volunteer in a licensed nuclear medicine department

questions.explanation: The 0.1 rem annual public dose limit is calculated exclusive of background radiation, any radioactive material the individual has received as a patient, exposure from individuals who have received radioactive material, and voluntary participation in medical research programs. Radiation received while volunteering or working in a licensed department is not listed as an excluded source and would count toward the public limit if that individual is not a classified radiation worker.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources must not exceed which of the following limits?
questions.explanation: To protect the public, the dose in any unrestricted area from external sources must not exceed 2 mrem in any 1 hour and 50 mrem per year. The 2 mrem/hr hourly limit is the same threshold that defines the upper boundary of an unrestricted area. The 50 mrem/year external source limit is distinct from the broader 100 mrem/year total public dose limit, which encompasses all licensed operation contributions.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes a "declared pregnant worker"?

choices.text: A worker who has voluntarily informed their employer in writing of their pregnancy and estimated date of conception
Any radiation worker who is known by their employer to be pregnant, regardless of how that information was shared
A worker who has filed a formal declaration with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) directly
A worker whose pregnancy has been confirmed by an occupational health physician and reported to the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)

questions.explanation: A declared pregnant worker is specifically defined as one who has voluntarily informed their employer, in writing, of the pregnancy and the estimated date of conception. Verbal notification is not sufficient. The declaration is voluntary, and the worker retains the right not to declare the pregnancy if she chooses. A separate written declaration is required for each pregnancy.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: How many written pregnancy declarations are required if a radiation worker becomes pregnant on two separate occasions during her career?

choices.text: One per facility; if she changes employers, a new declaration is required
None; pregnancy declarations must be filed by the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO), not the worker
One; a single declaration covers all future pregnancies
Two; a separate written declaration must be submitted for each pregnancy

questions.explanation: A separate written declaration must be submitted for each pregnancy. The declaration is specific to a single gestational period and does not carry over to subsequent pregnancies. Each declaration must include the estimated date of conception and is submitted voluntarily by the worker to her employer.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about a radiation worker's right to declare or not declare a pregnancy is correct?

choices.text: A worker may choose not to declare a pregnancy, in which case the embryo/fetus dose limits do not apply
All pregnant radiation workers are required by regulation to declare their pregnancy
The employer may require a worker to declare a pregnancy if pregnancy is suspected
A worker must declare the pregnancy to both her employer and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)

questions.explanation: Declaration of pregnancy is entirely voluntary. A worker may decide not to declare the pregnancy, in which case the regulatory embryo/fetus dose limits do not apply. The decision not to declare may be made for a variety of personal or professional reasons. Employers may not require declaration, and the NRC does not need to be notified directly by the worker.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: A radiation worker declared her pregnancy at 10 weeks gestation. She is now at 24 weeks and is concerned that dose restrictions will require her to change her work assignment, which she prefers to avoid. Which of the following options is available to her?

choices.text: She must be reassigned by her employer once the dose approaches the limit, regardless of her preference
She may only de-declare with written approval from the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) and the authorized user
She may request a temporary Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) waiver to allow doses above the embryo/fetus limit
She may de-declare her pregnancy at any time, removing the regulatory embryo/fetus dose constraint

questions.explanation: A declared pregnant worker may de-declare her pregnancy at any time. This option exists specifically for situations in which the embryo/fetus dose may approach limits and the worker does not wish to change her place of work or stop working. De-declaration removes the regulatory embryo/fetus dose constraints. No RSO approval or NRC waiver is required for de-declaration.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: A radiation worker declares her pregnancy late in gestation. At the time of declaration, the dose to the embryo/fetus is already 0.47 rem - within 0.05 rem of the 0.5 rem limit. Under which condition will the licensee be deemed in compliance?

choices.text: The licensee is automatically in violation because the limit was approached before declaration
The licensee must file a written report with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) within 15 days
The licensee is in compliance if the additional dose during the remainder of the pregnancy does not exceed 0.05 rem
The licensee is in compliance only if the worker immediately ceases all radiation work

questions.explanation: If the dose to the embryo/fetus is found to have exceeded 0.5 rem or is within 0.05 rem of the limit by the time of declaration, the licensee is still deemed to be in compliance - provided that the additional dose during the remainder of the pregnancy does not exceed 0.05 rem. This provision protects both workers who declare late and licensees, recognizing that dose may accrue before a worker chooses to formally declare.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which workers are required by regulation to receive adequate training to protect themselves against radiation?

choices.text: All individuals who, in the course of employment, are likely to receive a dose exceeding 100 mrem per year
All radiation workers, regardless of expected exposure level
All personnel who work in or adjacent to a nuclear medicine department
All personnel who handle radiopharmaceuticals directly

questions.explanation: Individuals who, in the course of their employment, are likely to receive a dose of more than 100 mrem per year must receive adequate training to protect themselves against radiation. These individuals also have the right to know the amount of radiation to which they have been exposed, and the right to request an Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) inspection if they believe their work environment has radiation safety problems.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: If a radiation worker believes their work environment has radiation safety problems, they have the right to:

choices.text: Submit a complaint directly to the Department of Transportation
Refuse work assignments until the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) conducts an internal audit
Request that the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) conduct an inspection of the facility
Request an immediate review by the radiation safety committee

questions.explanation: Radiation workers have the right to ask the NRC to conduct an inspection if they believe their working environment has safety problems. This is a federally protected right, separate from any internal facility processes such as RSO audits or Radiation Safety Committee (RSC) reviews. Workers also have the right to know their radiation exposure history.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Individual monitoring for occupational radiation exposure is required for adults who are likely to receive what fraction of the applicable dose limits from external sources in a year?
questions.explanation: Individual monitoring is required for adults who are likely to receive more than 10% of the annual occupational dose limits from external sources in a year. This same 10% threshold applies to dosimeter requirements described elsewhere in the radiation protection program. Monitoring is also required for any individual entering a high or very high radiation area.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Individual monitoring is required for minors who are likely to receive a whole-body dose from external radiation sources exceeding which level in a year?
questions.explanation: Individual monitoring is required for minors likely to receive more than 100 mrem from external radiation sources in a year. A lens dose equivalent exceeding 150 mrem or a shallow-dose equivalent to the skin or extremities exceeding 500 mrem also each independently trigger the monitoring requirement for minors. These thresholds reflect proportionate fractions of the minor dose limits.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Individual monitoring is required for minors who are likely to receive a lens dose equivalent exceeding which level in a year?
questions.explanation: Individual monitoring is required for minors likely to receive a lens dose equivalent in excess of 150 mrem in a year. This is distinct from the whole-body threshold for minors (100 mrem) and the skin/extremity threshold (500 mrem). The 1500 mrem value represents the minor annual eye lens dose limit, not the monitoring trigger.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Individual monitoring is required for minors who are likely to receive a shallow-dose equivalent to the skin or extremities exceeding which level in a year?
questions.explanation: Individual monitoring is required for minors likely to receive a shallow-dose equivalent to the skin or extremities in excess of 500 mrem from external radiation in a year. This threshold is higher than the whole-body (100 mrem) and lens (150 mrem) triggers for minors, reflecting the higher annual dose limit for skin and extremities compared to the whole body and eye lens.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Individual monitoring is required for a declared pregnant worker who is likely to receive what level of dose from external sources during the entire pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Individual monitoring is required for a declared pregnant worker likely to receive more than 100 mrem during the entire pregnancy from external radiation sources. This threshold is notably lower than the 0.5 rem embryo/fetus dose limit itself, ensuring that monitoring is in place well before the limit is approached.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: An Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) reviewing radiation badge readings initiates a formal investigation when a radiation worker exceeds 10% of the occupational exposure limit in which time period?
questions.explanation: An RSO initiates an investigation when a radiation worker exceeds 10% of the occupational exposure limit in a quarter. The investigation includes evaluation of adherence to as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) principles and proper badge placement. Note that this quarterly 10% trigger is distinct from the annual 10% threshold that determines whether individual monitoring is required in the first place.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: When an Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) investigates elevated radiation badge readings, the investigation specifically evaluates which of the following?

choices.text: Whether the facility's shielding meets current Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) standards
Whether the worker has a prior history of overexposure in Radiation Exposure Information and Reporting System (REIRS)
Whether the authorized user's license needs to be amended
Adherence to as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) principles and proper badge placement

questions.explanation: When a radiation worker exceeds 10% of the occupational exposure limit in a quarter, the RSO's investigation evaluates adherence to the principles of ALARA and proper badge placement. These two factors are the most common modifiable causes of elevated occupational dose and are directly within the facility's control.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT required to be included in the records of doses received by individually monitored workers?

choices.text: Shallow-dose equivalent to the skin and to the extremities
The worker's total career radiation dose prior to employment at the current facility
Deep-dose equivalent to the whole body

questions.explanation: Required dose record elements include the deep-dose equivalent to the whole body, lens dose equivalent, shallow-dose equivalent to the skin, shallow-dose equivalent to the extremities, estimated intake of radionuclides, and effective whole-body and organ dose. Prior career dose history at other facilities is not a required element of the current licensee's records, though such histories may be accessible through the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)'s Radiation Exposure Information and Reporting System (REIRS) database.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: At a minimum, how frequently must a licensee make entries into individual radiation dose records?

choices.text: Only when doses approach 10% of the quarterly limit

questions.explanation: The licensee must make entries into individual dose records at least annually and maintain clear, legible records. Records must be protected from public disclosure due to their personal privacy nature. The dose records for an embryo/fetus are maintained with the records of the declared pregnant worker, while the pregnancy declaration itself may be maintained separately.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The dose records for an embryo/fetus must be maintained:

choices.text: In a file submitted directly to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Regional Office
Separately from all other records, in a confidential file maintained by the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)
With the records of the authorized user who approved the worker's assignments
With the dose records of the declared pregnant worker

questions.explanation: The dose records for the embryo/fetus must be maintained with the dose records of the declared pregnant worker. The declaration of pregnancy may be kept on file separately from the dose records. Both types of records are protected from public disclosure because of their personal privacy nature.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Organizations requesting radiation dose histories from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)'s Radiation Exposure Information and Reporting System (REIRS) may submit requests for up to how many individuals at one time?
questions.explanation: Organizations and individuals may request dose histories from REIRS for up to 10 individuals at a time. The requestor must provide their own identifying information as well as the identification number, name, and date of birth of each monitored individual being queried. REIRS is the NRC's central repository for annual worker dose equivalent exposure data reported by licensees.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The assigned shallow-dose equivalent for the skin must represent the dose averaged over which area?

choices.text: The 100 sq cm of skin receiving the highest dose
The contiguous 10 sq cm of skin receiving the highest exposure
The 1 sq cm of skin receiving the highest dose

questions.explanation: The assigned shallow-dose equivalent must be the dose averaged over the contiguous 10 sq cm of skin receiving the highest exposure. Similarly, the deep-dose equivalent is assigned to the part of the body receiving the highest exposure. Both may be assessed from surveys or other radiation measurements for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with occupational dose limits.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Doses received in excess of annual occupational limits, including those from accidents or emergencies, must be subtracted from the limits for planned special exposures during which time periods?

choices.text: The remainder of the current calendar quarter and the following quarter
The next 5 years of the individual's occupational history
The current year and during the individual's lifetime

questions.explanation: Doses received in excess of annual limits, including those from accidents, emergencies, and planned special exposures, must be subtracted from the limits for planned special exposures that the individual may receive during the current year and during the individual's lifetime. This cumulative accounting ensures that planned elevated exposures cannot be used to circumvent the spirit of dose limits following an overexposure event.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: The assigned deep-dose equivalent for occupational dose record purposes must represent the dose to which part of the body?

choices.text: The part of the body closest to the radiation source
An average of all monitored body regions
The part of the body receiving the highest exposure
The torso, regardless of the location of highest exposure

questions.explanation: The assigned deep-dose equivalent must be for the part of the body receiving the highest exposure. This parallels the rule for shallow-dose equivalent, which must be averaged over the contiguous 10 sq cm of skin receiving the highest dose. Both values may be assessed from surveys or other radiation measurements for the purpose of demonstrating compliance with occupational dose limits.

questions.chapterName: Section 4: Regulatory Exposure Limits to Radioactive Materials
questions.stem: Licensees are required to provide the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) with reports of their workers' individual dose equivalent exposures at what frequency?

choices.text: Only when a worker exceeds 10% of the applicable dose limit

questions.explanation: Licensees are required to provide the NRC with an annual report of their workers' individual dose equivalent exposures. The NRC maintains this data in its Radiation Exposure Information and Reporting System (REIRS), which serves as a central resource for responding to workers' requests for their own exposure information and dose histories. The annual reporting cycle is distinct from the quarterly monitoring review threshold that triggers Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) investigation.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Each syringe or vial containing unsealed radioactive byproduct material must be labeled to do which of the following?

choices.text: Display the radiation warning symbol and dose rate at 30 cm
Show the patient's name and date of birth
Identify the authorized user who ordered the dose

questions.explanation: Each syringe or vial containing unsealed radioactive byproduct material must be labeled to identify the radiopharmaceutical. The label serves as primary identification of what the container holds. Patient name is not required on most syringe/vial labels at the time of dispensing for diagnostic dosing - a 72-hour exemption allows time to associate the patient's name with the prescription after dispensing. Radiation dose rate and authorized user identification are not standard syringe/vial labeling requirements.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: When is it NOT required to label a syringe shield used with a radioactive syringe?

choices.text: When the shield is used only for transport and not administration
When the procedure is performed by an authorized user directly
When the label on the syringe itself is visible when shielded
When the shield is made of tungsten rather than lead

questions.explanation: Syringe/vial shields must be labeled unless the label on the syringe or vial is visible when shielded. If the underlying container label can be read through or around the shield, a separate label on the shield is not required. The type of shielding material and who is performing the procedure are not factors in this labeling requirement.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a required element of a radiopharmaceutical dosage label?

choices.text: The amount of radiopharmaceutical and date/time of measurement
The name, address, and telephone number of the dispensing nuclear pharmacy
The radiopharmaceutical radionuclide and chemical form

questions.explanation: The required elements of a radiopharmaceutical dosage label include: the radiopharmaceutical radionuclide and chemical form; the amount and date/time of measurement; the expiration date and time; quantity (volume, capsule number/weight, or ampules/vials/syringes for gases); the name, address, and telephone number of the dispensing nuclear pharmacy; the prescription or lot number; and the name of the radiopharmaceutical. A patient's social security number is not a required label element.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: A radiopharmaceutical dosage label must include expiration information at what level of specificity?

choices.text: Expiration date and the activity at expiration
Expiration date, time, and authorized user name

questions.explanation: The radiopharmaceutical dosage label must include both the expiration date and expiration time. This level of specificity matters because short-lived radiopharmaceuticals can change substantially in activity over hours, and the time of expiration is needed to ensure the dose is used within its valid window. The authorized user's name and activity at expiration are not required label elements.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: For which types of radiopharmaceutical dispensing is the patient's name required on the label at the time of dispensing?

choices.text: Any radiopharmaceutical with an activity greater than 30 mCi
All radiopharmaceuticals requiring a written directive

questions.explanation: Labels for radiolabeled blood components and radiotherapies must contain the patient's name at the time of dispensing. For diagnostic dosing, a 72-hour exemption exists when the patient's name is not yet available - the name must be associated with the prescription within 72 hours and retained for 3 years. Activity thresholds and written directive requirements are not the criteria that determine whether a patient name is required on the label at the time of dispensing.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: When a diagnostic radiopharmaceutical is dispensed and the patient's name is not yet available, what is the maximum time allowed to associate the patient's name with the prescription?
questions.explanation: A 72-hour exemption is allowed when the patient's name is not available at the time of dispensing for diagnostic dosing. No later than 72 hours after dispensing, the patient's name must be associated with the prescription in a readily retrievable manner. This exemption does not apply to radiolabeled blood components or radiotherapies, for which the patient name must be on the label at the time of dispensing.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: For how long must the record associating a patient's name with a diagnostic radiopharmaceutical prescription be retained?
questions.explanation: Once the patient's name has been associated with the diagnostic radiopharmaceutical prescription (within the 72-hour window), that record must be retained for 3 years. This retention period is consistent with other survey and disposal records throughout the regulations.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: In addition to the standard syringe/vial label, which of the following items must be included for administered radiopharmaceuticals?

choices.text: The name and address of the nuclear pharmacy, the name of the authorized user, and the lot number of the preparation
The patient's diagnosis and treating institution name
The referring physician's name and pager number
The radiation dose rate at the time of administration

questions.explanation: For administered radiopharmaceuticals, the following additional items must be included: the name and address of the nuclear pharmacy, the name of the end authorized user (who is also the prescriber), and the lot number of the preparation. The referring physician's contact information, dose rate at administration, and patient diagnosis are not required additional labeling elements.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What must be affixed to the delivery container when dispensing radiopharmaceuticals?

choices.text: A chain-of-custody seal signed by the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)

questions.explanation: A tamper-evident seal must be affixed to the delivery container when dispensing radiopharmaceuticals. This requirement applies to the container in which the radiopharmaceutical is delivered, not to the syringe or vial directly or to the shipping paperwork.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: By what percentage is the administered radiopharmaceutical dosage permitted to vary from the prescribed dosage without the licensee being cited?
questions.explanation: The administered dosage is permitted to vary from the prescribed dosage by ±20%. If the licensee is aware that the administered dosage differs from the prescribed dosage by more than 20% and administers it anyway, the licensee would be cited. However, an authorized user may direct an administered dosage more than 20% outside the prescribed range for medical purposes, provided the authorized user modifies the prescription to encompass the new dosage.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: An authorized user wishes to administer a dose 30% below the prescribed dosage range for medical reasons. Which of the following is required?

choices.text: The authorized user must modify the prescription to encompass the new dosage to be administered
Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) notification within 24 hours
The licensee must document the deviation but may proceed without changing the prescription
The dose must be withheld and the referring provider notified

questions.explanation: When an authorized user directs an administered dosage that is more than 20% outside the prescribed range for medical purposes, the authorized user must modify the prescription - revising it from the original prescribed dosage or dosage range to a revised range that encompasses the dosage to be administered. NRC notification is not required for this type of authorized deviation, and the dose may proceed once the prescription is updated.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: For a unit dosage radiopharmaceutical, how must the activity be determined before administration?

choices.text: By direct measurement of radioactivity or decay correction based on initial activity from a licensed manufacturer
By any method approved in writing by the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)
By mathematical calculation from dispensed volume only

questions.explanation: For a unit dosage, the activity determination must be made by direct measurement of radioactivity or by decay correction based on the initial activity as determined by a licensed manufacturer. For non-unit dosages, acceptable methods also include a combination of measurement and mathematical calculations, or volumetric measurements and mathematical calculations. The licensee must retain a record of the dosage determination.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: For a non-unit radiopharmaceutical dosage, which of the following is an acceptable method of activity determination before administration?

choices.text: Manufacturer's stated nominal activity without further measurement or calculation
A combination of volumetric measurements and mathematical calculations
Visual inspection of the syringe fill level
Decay correction from a licensed manufacturer's predetermined activity alone

questions.explanation: For non-unit dosages, acceptable determination methods include direct measurement of radioactivity, a combination of measurement and mathematical calculations, or volumetric measurements and mathematical calculations from the manufacturer. Decay correction from a licensed manufacturer's predetermined activity is specifically the method reserved for unit dosages, not non-unit dosages. Visual inspection is not an accepted method.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: How many patient identifiers must be confirmed before administering a radiopharmaceutical?

choices.text: Two for diagnostic procedures, three for therapeutic procedures

questions.explanation: Before any radiopharmaceutical administration, the patient's identity must be confirmed with two patient identifiers. This applies regardless of whether the administration is diagnostic or therapeutic. The requirement for two identifiers reduces the risk of wrong-patient errors.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an approved patient identifier for radiopharmaceutical administration?
questions.explanation: Approved patient identifiers include the individual's name, assigned identification number, telephone number, date of birth, person-specific identifiers, and electronic identification technology (such as bar coding or radio frequency identification (RFID)) containing two or more person-specific identifiers. Room number is not an approved identifier because it is not person-specific - room assignments change and can be shared.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Electronic identification technology qualifies as a patient identifier for radiopharmaceutical administration only if it meets which requirement?

choices.text: It must be approved by the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) and listed in the radiation protection program
It must link to the patient's electronic medical record
It must be verified by the authorized user before each administration
It must include two or more person-specific identifiers

questions.explanation: Electronic identification technology such as bar coding or radio frequency identification (RFID) qualifies as a patient identifier only if it includes two or more person-specific identifiers. A single identifier embedded in electronic format does not meet the two-identifier standard. The technology must encode sufficient redundancy to confirm patient identity.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: When a patient's identity cannot be verified before radiopharmaceutical administration, what is the required approach?

choices.text: Two staff members must jointly attest to the patient's identity
A temporary means of identification must be used, with formal identification obtained as soon as possible
The authorized user must personally identify the patient before proceeding
The administration must be postponed until full identification is confirmed

questions.explanation: When a patient's identity cannot be verified, a temporary means of identification must be used and formal identification should occur as soon as possible. When obtained, the new identifying information should be used. The regulations note that no standards exist for the use of an alias to protect anonymity, and organizations should evaluate risks and utilize two identifiers regardless.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Inadvertent administration of byproduct material to a pregnant patient results in a 6 rem dose to the embryo/fetus. By when must the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Operations Center be notified by telephone?

choices.text: No later than the next calendar day after discovery

questions.explanation: Licensees must notify the NRC Operations Center by telephone no later than the next calendar day after discovery of a dose to an embryo/fetus that meets reporting criteria. The reportable threshold is a dose greater than 5 rem (50 mSv) resulting from byproduct administration to a pregnant individual, unless specifically approved in advance by the authorized user.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What is the embryo/fetus dose threshold above which Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) notification is required following inadvertent byproduct administration to a pregnant patient?
questions.explanation: A dose to an embryo/fetus greater than 5 rem (50 mSv) resulting from byproduct administration to a pregnant individual must be reported to the NRC, unless the dose was specifically approved in advance by the authorized user. This is the dose equivalent to the embryo/fetus, not the dose to the mother.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: By when must a written report be submitted to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Regional Office after discovery of a reportable embryo/fetus or nursing child dose event?
questions.explanation: Following a reportable dose to an embryo/fetus or nursing child, the licensee must submit a written report to the NRC Regional Office within 15 days of discovery. This is separate from the telephone notification to the NRC Operations Center, which must occur no later than the next calendar day. Both forms of notification are required.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Which of the following must be included in the written report to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Regional Office after a reportable embryo/fetus dose event?

choices.text: The patient's full name and medical record number
The patient's prior radiation dose history
Certification that the licensee notified the pregnant individual or mother, or the reason why not
The names of all staff members present at the time of administration

questions.explanation: Required elements of the written report include: the licensee's name; the prescribing physician's name; a brief description of the event; the reason the event occurred; the effect on the embryo/fetus or nursing child; actions taken or planned to prevent recurrence; and certification that the licensee notified the pregnant individual or mother (or responsible relative/guardian), or the reason notification was not given. Importantly, the report must NOT include the individual's or child's name or any other identifying information.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Which of the following information must be EXCLUDED from the written Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) report following a reportable embryo/fetus dose event?

choices.text: A description of why the event occurred
The individual's or child's name or identifying information

questions.explanation: The written report must not include the individual's or child's name or any other identifying information for the individual or child. All other listed items - the prescribing physician's name, description of why the event occurred, and planned corrective actions - are required elements of the report. This privacy protection applies specifically to the affected patient and child.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: No later than when must the licensee notify the referring provider and the pregnant individual or mother after discovering a reportable embryo/fetus dose event?
questions.explanation: The licensee must notify the referring provider and the pregnant individual or mother no later than 24 hours after discovery of a reportable event. However, the licensee is not required to notify the mother without first consulting with the referring provider. If the referring provider will inform the mother, or if medical judgment indicates notification would be harmful, the licensee may defer.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Under which circumstance may a licensee defer direct notification of a pregnant patient following a reportable embryo/fetus dose event?

choices.text: When the patient is a minor and a guardian is not immediately available
When the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has already been notified by telephone
When the dose did not exceed 10 rem to the embryo/fetus
When the referring provider states they will notify the patient, or that notification would be medically harmful

questions.explanation: The licensee may defer notification of the pregnant individual or mother if the referring provider personally informs the licensee either that they will inform the mother, or that - based on medical judgment - telling the mother would be harmful. The licensee is not required to notify the mother without first consulting the referring provider. If the provider or mother cannot be reached within 24 hours, the licensee must notify as soon as possible thereafter.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: After a reportable embryo/fetus dose event, may the licensee delay appropriate medical care for the embryo/fetus pending completion of required notifications?

choices.text: No, but only for doses exceeding 10 rem
No; the licensee may not delay appropriate medical care because of any delay in notification
Yes, notifications must be completed before any additional interventions
Yes, but only if the delay is less than 24 hours

questions.explanation: The licensee may not delay any appropriate medical care - including any necessary remedial care - for the embryo/fetus or nursing child because of any delay in the notification process. Medical care takes priority. This applies regardless of the dose level involved.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What dose to a nursing child - resulting from administration of byproduct material to the breastfeeding mother - triggers a required Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) report?

choices.text: Any detectable dose absorbed by the nursing child
Greater than 5 rem TEDE, or any dose resulting in unintended permanent functional damage to an organ or physiological system
Greater than 1 rem total effective dose equivalent (TEDE)

questions.explanation: A reportable nursing child event occurs when the dose exceeds 5 rem (50 mSv) TEDE resulting from byproduct administration to the breastfeeding mother, or when the dose has caused unintended permanent functional damage to an organ or physiological system of the child as determined by a physician. The functional damage criterion can trigger reporting even at doses below 5 rem.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: A nursing mother who has received unsealed byproduct material may be released if the total effective dose equivalent projected to the nursing child does not exceed which level?
questions.explanation: A nursing mother who has received unsealed byproduct material can be released if the total effective dose equivalent to any other individual, including the nursing child, is projected not to exceed 500 mrem (5 mSv). This is distinct from the 100 mrem threshold that triggers the requirement to give written instructions to the mother about breastfeeding interruption.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Written instructions about breastfeeding interruption must be provided to a nursing mother when the nursing child's projected radiation exposure could exceed which level?
questions.explanation: If the nursing mother continues to breastfeed after receiving a radiopharmaceutical and the nursing child's radiation exposure could exceed an effective dose equivalent of 100 mrem (1 mSv), written instructions must be given to the mother. These instructions must address the potential adverse consequences if breastfeeding is not interrupted or ceased, as well as guidance on discontinuation. This 100 mrem trigger is lower than the 500 mrem release threshold.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: For a nursing mother about to undergo radioiodine therapy, oral and written radiation precaution instructions must be provided at least how far in advance of the procedure?
questions.explanation: Before radioiodine therapy, oral and written radiation precaution instructions must be provided to the nursing mother and appropriate family/caretakers at least six weeks prior to the radioiodine procedure. This advance notice allows sufficient time for lactation cessation before therapy, which is necessary to minimize radiation dose to the breast tissue.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies following administration of 18F for a positron emission tomography (PET) scan?
questions.explanation: Following administration of 18F, a 4-hour breastfeeding interruption is recommended. This short interruption reflects the brief physical half-life of 18F (approximately 110 minutes). By contrast, 99mTc-labeled radiopharmaceuticals require a 24-hour interruption, and 123I-NaI requires a 3-day interruption.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: A patient undergoing a 67Ga scan is breastfeeding. What is the recommended breastfeeding interruption period?
questions.explanation: Administration of 67Ga requires a 28-day breastfeeding interruption. This extended period reflects the relatively long physical half-life of 67Ga (approximately 78 hours) and its significant excretion into breast milk. This is among the longest interruption periods for diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals, exceeded only by agents requiring permanent cessation.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies following administration of 68Ga?
questions.explanation: No breastfeeding interruption is required following administration of 68Ga. Despite sharing the gallium element with 67Ga (which requires 28 days), 68Ga has an ultrashort physical half-life of approximately 68 minutes, making clinically significant breast milk contamination negligible. Other agents also requiring no interruption include 13N and 82Rb.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: A breastfeeding patient is scheduled to receive 123I-NaI for a thyroid scan. What interruption of breastfeeding is recommended?

choices.text: Permanent cessation for the current child

questions.explanation: A 3-day breastfeeding interruption is recommended following administration of 123I-NaI. This is distinct from the recommendation for 131I-NaI and 124I-NaI, which require permanent cessation of breastfeeding for the current child. The shorter interruption for 123I reflects its significantly lower dose burden compared to the therapeutic iodine isotopes.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies to a patient who has received 131I-NaI for thyroid ablation?

choices.text: No interruption if the administered activity is less than 30 mCi
Permanent cessation for the current child

questions.explanation: Administration of 131I-NaI requires permanent cessation of breastfeeding for the current child. The same recommendation applies to 124I-NaI. Additionally, breastfeeding should be stopped six weeks prior to 131I therapy to minimize radiation dose to the breast tissue itself. This is one of the most stringent breastfeeding recommendations in nuclear medicine.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies to a patient who has received 124I-NaI?

choices.text: Permanent cessation for the current child

questions.explanation: Administration of 124I-NaI requires permanent cessation of breastfeeding for the current child, the same recommendation as for 131I-NaI. Although 124I is often used diagnostically in positron emission tomography (PET) imaging, it carries the same breastfeeding recommendation as 131I due to iodine's concentration in breast milk. Breastfeeding should also be stopped six weeks prior to the procedure.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: How far in advance of 131I or 124I therapy must a breastfeeding patient stop nursing to minimize radiation dose to the breast?
questions.explanation: Breastfeeding should be stopped six weeks prior to 131I-NaI or 124I-NaI therapy to minimize radiation dose to the breast. This recommendation exists because radioiodine concentrates in breast tissue, and pre-procedure cessation reduces this uptake. Oral and written precaution instructions should be provided to the nursing mother at least six weeks before the procedure to allow adequate time for lactation cessation.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies following administration of 111In-labeled white blood cells?
questions.explanation: A 6-day breastfeeding interruption is recommended following administration of 111In-labeled white blood cells. This is longer than the 4-day interruption for 201Tl-chloride and the 24-hour interruption for 99mTc-labeled agents, reflecting the longer physical half-life of 111In (approximately 67 hours) and its excretion into breast milk.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies to a patient treated with 177Lu-dotatate?

choices.text: No interruption if activity is less than 200 mCi
Permanent cessation for the current child

questions.explanation: Administration of 177Lu-dotatate requires permanent cessation of breastfeeding for the current child. This is the same recommendation as for 131I-NaI and 124I-NaI. 177Lu-dotatate is a targeted radionuclide therapy for somatostatin receptor-positive tumors, and its secretion into breast milk at therapeutic activities makes permanent cessation necessary.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies following administration of 13N?
questions.explanation: No breastfeeding interruption is required following administration of 13N. The ultrashort half-life of 13N (approximately 10 minutes) results in essentially complete decay before any significant breast milk exposure can occur. Other agents also requiring no interruption include 68Ga and 82Rb.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies following administration of 82Rb?
questions.explanation: No breastfeeding interruption is required following administration of 82Rb. 82Rb has an ultrashort physical half-life of approximately 76 seconds, making clinically significant breast milk contamination negligible. 68Ga and 13N are the other commonly used agents for which no breastfeeding interruption is required.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies following administration of any 99mTc-labeled radiopharmaceutical?
questions.explanation: A 24-hour breastfeeding interruption is recommended following administration of all 99mTc-labeled radiopharmaceuticals. This recommendation applies across the entire class of 99mTc compounds, regardless of the specific agent. The physical half-life of 99mTc is approximately 6 hours, and a 24-hour interruption represents approximately four half-lives.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What breastfeeding recommendation applies following administration of 201Tl-chloride?
questions.explanation: A 4-day breastfeeding interruption is recommended following administration of 201Tl-chloride. This is longer than the 24-hour interruption for 99mTc agents and shorter than the 6-day interruption for 111In-labeled white blood cells. The physical half-life of 201Tl is approximately 73 hours, and its significant excretion into breast milk necessitates an extended interruption period.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: For a patient receiving brachytherapy or radioactive seed localization, what is the recommended approach to breastfeeding?

choices.text: Breastfeeding should be suspended while radioactive seeds are in place and may resume after their removal
A 28-day interruption is required after seed placement regardless of when seeds are removed
No interruption is required as long as seeds are not implanted near the breast

questions.explanation: Brachytherapy and radioactive seed localization procedures generally require suspension of breastfeeding while the radioactive seeds are in place. Breastfeeding may resume after the seeds are removed. This contrasts with systemic radiopharmaceutical administration, where recommendations are based on physical half-life and clearance from breast milk.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: A nursing mother is treated with 90Y-microspheres via radioembolic therapy. What is the recommended approach to breastfeeding?

choices.text: Permanent cessation for the current child

questions.explanation: Radioembolic therapy with 90Y-microspheres does not require breastfeeding interruption. This is because 90Y does not enter systemic circulation, breast tissue, or breast milk. The microspheres are physically lodged in the tumor vasculature and do not redistribute systemically, eliminating the route of exposure that applies to systemically distributed radionuclides.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Why does 90Y-microsphere therapy not require breastfeeding interruption, unlike most radionuclide therapies?

choices.text: 90Y does not enter systemic circulation, breast tissue, or breast milk
The activity administered is below the threshold that poses risk to the nursing child
The nursing child's dose from breast milk is diluted to below the 100 mrem threshold
90Y emits only alpha particles, which cannot reach the breast tissue

questions.explanation: The reason 90Y-microsphere radioembolic therapy does not require breastfeeding interruption is that 90Y does not enter systemic circulation, breast tissue, or breast milk. The microspheres are physically trapped in the tumor vasculature. 90Y is actually a pure beta emitter (not an alpha emitter), and the key distinction here is its non-systemic distribution rather than its particle type.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Individuals involved in administering volatile 131I radiopharmaceuticals may be sampled for bioassay when the administered activity exceeds which threshold?
questions.explanation: Individuals involved in administering volatile 131I radiopharmaceuticals may be sampled for bioassay if the administered activity exceeds 10 mCi. Volatile radioiodine poses an inhalation risk to handlers, and bioassay sampling evaluates internal uptake in those who administer higher activities.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Which syringe shield material is preferred for administering positron-emitting radiopharmaceuticals, and why?

choices.text: Tungsten; because it provides better attenuation at smaller thickness, is lighter, and is less toxic than lead
Aluminum; because it is the most cost-effective shielding option available
Lead; because it provides the highest atomic number and best photon attenuation
Acrylic; because it prevents bremsstrahlung from positron annihilation photons

questions.explanation: Tungsten is the preferred syringe shield material for positron emitters. It provides better radiation attenuation at a smaller thickness than lead, allowing for a lighter and more manageable shield, and it is less toxic than lead. Lead is still used in some applications as a more cost-effective option, but tungsten is preferred. Acrylic and aluminum are not appropriate for shielding the 511 keV annihilation photons produced by positron emitters.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Why is lead an ineffective primary shielding material for beta-emitting radiopharmaceuticals?

choices.text: Lead's density causes beta particles to scatter rather than be absorbed
Lead is too expensive compared to alternatives
Lead reacts chemically with common beta-emitting radiopharmaceuticals
The interaction of beta particles with lead produces bremsstrahlung radiation, generating additional exposure

questions.explanation: Lead is an ineffective primary shield for beta emitters because beta particles interacting with the high-atomic-number lead produce bremsstrahlung (braking radiation), which generates additional X-ray exposure rather than reducing total exposure. Lower atomic number materials such as acrylic or aluminum are preferred for beta emitter shielding because they stop the beta particles with minimal bremsstrahlung production.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Which shielding materials are appropriate for beta-emitting radiopharmaceuticals?
questions.explanation: Acrylic (plastic) and aluminum are appropriate shielding materials for beta emitters because they are low atomic number materials that stop beta particles while producing minimal bremsstrahlung. Lead and tungsten - preferred for gamma and X-ray shielding - are avoided for pure beta emitters because their high atomic numbers produce significant bremsstrahlung upon beta interaction.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Where on the hand should a finger (ring) dosimeter be worn when administering radiopharmaceuticals?

choices.text: Over the glove, on the dominant hand, with the detector facing outward
Over the glove, on the index finger, with the detector facing the radiation source directly
Under the glove, on the finger most likely to be exposed, with the detector facing the palm
Under the glove, on the non-dominant hand, with the detector facing away from the palm

questions.explanation: Finger (ring) dosimeters should be worn under a glove, on the hand most likely to be exposed to radiation, on a finger exposed to radiation, with the detector (badge) facing the palm. Wearing the dosimeter under the glove protects it from contamination and keeps it in position. The palm-facing orientation positions the detector toward the source of exposure during syringe manipulation.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: After treating a radioactive inpatient, which articles must be surveyed for contamination before being removed from the room or held for decay-in-storage?

choices.text: Only items that contacted the patient's excreta
Only items that directly contacted the patient's skin
Bedding, clothing, towels, food, and food trays
Bedding and clothing only; food items are exempt from survey requirements

questions.explanation: After treatment, all articles including bedding, clothing, towels, food, and food trays must be surveyed for contamination before they are removed or held in storage for decay-in-storage. Food items are explicitly included in this requirement. The patient should also be surveyed before release and instructed on ways to minimize contamination and exposure.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Where should radionuclide generators be placed within a nuclear medicine facility?

choices.text: In a locked refrigerator accessible only to the authorized nuclear pharmacist
In the patient preparation area to minimize transport distance
Adjacent to the dose calibrator for efficient access during elution

questions.explanation: Radionuclide generators should be placed in a remote, well-shielded enclosure. This placement minimizes occupational exposure to staff during generator operation. Dose calibrators should also be shielded to protect workers, and lead shielding should be used for gamma-emitting radiopharmaceuticals such as 99mTc.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: For 133Xe ventilation studies, what specific additional shielding is required beyond standard precautions?

choices.text: A lead-lined room with a minimum of 2 inches of shielding in all walls
Additional lead shielding around the charcoal absorber canister, oxygen bag, and waste receptacle
Tungsten shielding around the xenon delivery system only
Lead shielding around the patient's head during the study

questions.explanation: For 133Xe studies, additional lead shielding is required around the charcoal absorber canister, oxygen bag, and waste receptacle to prevent exposure from these components of the xenon delivery system. Leakage or contamination from the radioactive material should be prevented. Individualized 133Xe room evacuation time calculations are also required in rooms where ventilation scans are performed.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: What calculation is specifically required in rooms where 133Xe ventilation scans are performed?

choices.text: A half-value layer calculation for 133Xe gamma emissions in the room walls
A dedicated negative-pressure ventilation rate verification
A continuous air monitoring threshold based on 10% of the occupational limit

questions.explanation: Individualized 133Xe room evacuation time calculations are required in rooms where ventilation scans are performed. These calculations are room-specific because ventilation rates and room volumes vary between facilities. The calculations determine how long it would take for 133Xe activity in the room to reach acceptable levels in the event of a release or spill.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: How should shielded waste containers holding radioactive syringes be positioned in the work area?

choices.text: As far as possible from the workers
Within arm's reach of the work surface to minimize transport distance
Centered in the room for equal accessibility by all workers
Adjacent to the dose calibrator to facilitate activity verification

questions.explanation: Shielded containers or waste cans used for syringes and other radioactive waste should be kept at as great a distance as possible from the workers. This applies the principle of distance as a radiation protection measure. The inconvenience of a more distant waste container is outweighed by the reduction in occupational exposure.

questions.chapterName: Section 5: Radiopharmaceutical Administration
questions.stem: Fume hoods should be used in nuclear medicine for which type of radioactive material?

choices.text: All gamma-emitting radiopharmaceuticals regardless of volatility
All radiopharmaceuticals administered in activities greater than 30 mCi

questions.explanation: Fume hoods should be used for potential airborne radioactive materials. This is particularly relevant for volatile compounds such as liquid 131I-NaI, 133Xe gas, and other volatile radiopharmaceuticals where inhalation is a significant exposure pathway. Fume hoods capture and exhaust radioactive vapors before they can be inhaled by staff.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which federal agency has regulatory authority over the possession and use of byproduct materials in nuclear medicine?

choices.text: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

questions.explanation: The NRC (or the responsible Agreement State) has regulatory authority over the possession and use of byproduct materials or other nuclear material in medicine. The FDA has a separate and distinct role: it oversees good manufacturing practices for radiopharmaceuticals, medical devices, and radiation-producing x-ray machines and accelerators. The two agencies thus have complementary but non-overlapping jurisdictions.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which federal agency oversees the manufacturing of radiopharmaceuticals, medical devices, and radiation-producing x-ray machines and accelerators?
questions.explanation: The FDA oversees good practices in the manufacturing of radiopharmaceuticals, medical devices, and radiation-producing x-ray machines and accelerators.
