The NRC's jurisdiction covers the possession and use of byproduct materials, not their manufacturing or the regulation of x-ray producing equipment.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: The legal mechanism by which the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) transfers portions of its regulatory authority to an Agreement State is:

choices.text: A resolution passed by the state legislature and ratified by the NRC
An agreement signed by the governor and the chair of the NRC commission
A memorandum of understanding between the state health department and the NRC regional office
A federal register rulemaking that delegates jurisdiction to the state

questions.explanation: The Atomic Energy Act of 1954 allows the NRC to relinquish portions of its regulatory authority to an Agreement State. The transfer mechanism is an agreement signed by the governor of the state and the chair of the NRC commission. As of the current study guide, 39 states have entered into such agreements.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: As of the current study period, how many states have entered into agreements with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to assume regulatory authority over byproduct materials?
questions.explanation: 39 states have entered into agreements with the NRC, becoming Agreement States. These states have assumed regulatory authority to license and regulate byproduct materials within their borders. The NRC retains authority in non-Agreement States and continues to coordinate with Agreement States on event reporting and allegations.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: The Integrated Materials Performance Evaluation Program (IMPEP) requires the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to do which of the following?

choices.text: Periodically review Agreement States to ensure their programs are adequate and compatible with NRC's regulatory program
Certify all RSOs working in Agreement States on a biennial basis
Publish annual comparative rankings of Agreement State programs
Inspect all radioactive material (RAM) licensees annually

questions.explanation: The IMPEP toolbox requires the NRC to periodically review Agreement States to ensure their radiation control programs are adequate to protect public health and safety and compatible with the NRC's regulatory program. This ongoing oversight ensures Agreement States maintain standards equivalent to those the NRC would apply directly.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: When must an Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) agree to be responsible for implementing the radiation protection program?

choices.text: In writing, before assuming the RSO role
Verbally at the time of appointment, with written confirmation within 30 days
Only upon initial hire; no ongoing agreement is required
At each annual Radiation Safety Committee (RSC) meeting where the program is reviewed

questions.explanation: The RSO agrees in writing to be responsible for implementing the radiation protection program. This written agreement is a regulatory requirement, not merely a best practice. Similarly, an associate RSO (ARSO) must be appointed in writing, and the RSO - with written agreement of licensee management - assigns specific duties and tasks to each ARSO.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: An associate Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) (ARSO) may be appointed to support the RSO. What is required for this appointment?

choices.text: The ARSO must hold the same board certifications as the RSO
The ARSO must be appointed in writing, with the RSO assigning duties using written agreement of licensee's management
Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approval of the ARSO designation within 30 days
The ARSO must be identified on the facility's radioactive material (RAM) license

questions.explanation: An ARSO may be appointed in writing to support the RSO. The RSO, with the written agreement of the licensee's management, must assign the specific duties and tasks to each ARSO. Importantly, the RSO shall not delegate the authority or responsibilities for implementing the radiation protection program itself - only specific tasks may be assigned to the ARSO.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which of the following responsibilities may the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) NOT delegate to an Associate Radiation Safety Officer (ARSO) or other staff member?

choices.text: Conducting routine area surveys in the nuclear medicine department
The authority and responsibilities for implementing the radiation protection program
Supervising the safe disposal of radioactive waste
Reviewing radiation badge readings for individual workers

questions.explanation: The RSO shall not delegate the authority or responsibilities for implementing the radiation protection program. While specific tasks (such as surveys, badge review, or waste disposal supervision) may be assigned to an ARSO or other appropriately trained personnel, the overall programmatic authority rests solely with the RSO and cannot be transferred. If an RSO or ARSO leaves or ceases to perform duties, the licensee must notify the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) or Agreement State.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: What is the minimum educational requirement for a candidate seeking Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) certification by an Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)-recognized specialty board?

choices.text: Associate's degree in any science discipline
Master's degree in health physics or a related field
Bachelor's degree in physical or biological science from an accredited college or university
Doctoral degree in physics, biology, or radiation science

questions.explanation: RSO candidates must hold at least a bachelor's degree from an accredited college or university in physical or biological science. They must also have 5 or more years of professional experience in health physics, including at least 3 years in applied health physics, and must pass an exam administered by diplomates of the specialty board.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: An Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) candidate has 6 years of total professional experience in health physics. How many of those years must be in applied health physics to meet the RSO qualification requirement?
questions.explanation: RSO candidates must have 5 or more years of professional experience in health physics, including at least 3 years in applied health physics. Applied health physics refers to hands-on, operational radiation safety work - such as performing surveys, calibrating instruments, handling radioactive materials, and managing decontamination - as distinguished from purely administrative or academic experience.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT among the specific authorities a licensee must provide to the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)?

choices.text: Terminate employment of non-compliant radiation workers

questions.explanation: The licensee must provide the RSO with sufficient authority, organizational freedom, time, resources, and management prerogative to: identify radiation safety problems; initiate, recommend, or provide corrective actions; stop unsafe operations; and verify implementation of corrective actions. The authority to terminate employment is not listed as a required RSO power - the RSO's authority is specifically directed at radiation safety operations, not personnel management.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: If an Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) leaves a licensee's employ, what action is required?

choices.text: The licensee must notify the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) or the responsible Agreement State
The licensee must submit a written report to the NRC within 30 days identifying a replacement candidate
The licensee must immediately suspend all radioactive material use until a new RSO is appointed
The licensee must appoint the most senior authorized user as acting RSO

questions.explanation: If an RSO or Associate Radiation Safety Officer (ARSO) leaves or ceases to perform their duties, the licensee needs to notify the NRC or Agreement State. The notification requirement applies to both the RSO and any ARSO. The regulations do not specify that operations must immediately cease - rather, the notification triggers the regulatory process for addressing the change in RSO status.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: An authorized user wishes to serve as the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) for their facility. In addition to meeting standard Authorized User (AU) criteria, which of the following is specifically required for this dual appointment?

choices.text: Written attestation from a preceptor RSO that the AU has achieved sufficient radiation safety knowledge to function independently as an RSO, plus written agreement to be responsible for the radiation protection program
At least 10 years of experience as an authorized user
Completion of a 700-hour RSO training program approved by the NRC
Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approval of the AU-as-RSO designation prior to assuming duties

questions.explanation: An AU may be appointed as the RSO if: the AU is identified as an AU on the license; has relevant radiation safety experience; has training in radiation safety, regulatory issues, and emergency procedures; and has obtained written attestation - signed by a preceptor RSO - that the AU has achieved sufficient radiation safety knowledge to function independently as an RSO for a medical use licensee. The AU must also agree, in writing, to be responsible for implementing the radiation protection program.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which of the following professionals is NOT eligible to qualify as an authorized user (AU) for medical use of byproduct material?
questions.explanation: An AU is a physician, dentist, or podiatrist who meets the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) criteria and is specified on the license. A pharmacist is not eligible to serve as an AU - a pharmacist who meets the appropriate criteria may qualify as an authorized nuclear pharmacist (ANP) instead, which is a distinct role with different responsibilities.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Is a license amendment required before a physician may begin work as an authorized user under an Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) license?

choices.text: Yes, but only if the physician will be performing therapeutic procedures
Yes; a license amendment must be submitted and approved before the physician begins work
No, but only if the physician holds board certification recognized by the NRC
No; a license amendment is not needed to permit the physician to begin work as an Authorized User (AU) under the NRC license

questions.explanation: A license amendment is not needed to permit the physician to begin work as an AU under the NRC license. However, for licensees other than those with a Type A specific license of broad scope, a copy of the Agreement State license would have to be submitted to the NRC within 30 days. The lack of a mandatory pre-approval amendment allows physicians to begin work more promptly once they meet the training and experience requirements.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Only which of the following individuals are permitted to use or prepare byproduct material in the practice of medicine?

choices.text: Authorized users and authorized nuclear pharmacists
Authorized users and authorized medical physicists
Radiation safety officers and authorized nuclear pharmacists
Authorized users and radiation safety officers

questions.explanation: Only authorized users (AUs) and authorized nuclear pharmacists (ANPs) are allowed to use or prepare, respectively, byproduct material in the practice of medicine. However, an Authorized User (AU) or Authorized Nuclear Pharmacist (ANP) may delegate specific tasks associated with the use or preparation of byproduct material to other individuals who are properly supervised and instructed. The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) and Authorized Medical Physicist (AMP) are not permitted to use or prepare byproduct material for medical use unless they also hold AU or ANP status.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: An individual may begin duties as an authorized nuclear pharmacist (ANP) if which of the following conditions is met?

choices.text: They hold a current state pharmacy license and have completed 200 hours of nuclear pharmacy training
They are identified as an ANP on an Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) or Agreement State medical use license or nuclear pharmacy license
They hold a doctorate in pharmacy and have completed a nuclear pharmacy residency
They have been nominated in writing by the facility's Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) and approved by the NRC regional office

questions.explanation: An individual can begin duties as an ANP as long as one of three conditions is met: (1) they meet board certification criteria and recentness of training requirements; (2) they are identified as an ANP on an NRC or Agreement State medical use license or nuclear pharmacy license; or (3) they are identified as an ANP by a commercial nuclear pharmacy authorized to identify ANPs. RSO nomination and pharmacy doctorates are not the regulatory criteria.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: An authorized medical physicist (AMP) must be named on the license for which of the following medical uses of byproduct material?

choices.text: Teletherapy units and photon-emitting remote after-loader units

questions.explanation: An AMP must be named on licenses authorizing the medical uses of 90Sr ophthalmic applicators, teletherapy units, photon-emitting remote after-loader units, and gamma stereotactic radiosurgery units. Diagnostic nuclear medicine procedures with 99mTc or 18F and brachytherapy procedures requiring an AMP would be those specific device types listed - not all brachytherapy sources.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Under which circumstance is a licensee required to have a radiation safety committee (RSC)?

choices.text: Whenever the licensee employs more than 10 radiation workers
Whenever the licensee is authorized for two or more different types of uses of byproduct material
Whenever the licensee conducts both diagnostic and therapeutic nuclear medicine procedures
Whenever the licensee has an annual occupational dose greater than 1 rem per worker

questions.explanation: Licensees authorized for two or more different types of uses of byproduct material must have an RSC to oversee all uses permitted by the license. The number of workers and overall dose levels are not the triggering criteria - it is specifically the diversity of authorized uses that mandates the RSC structure. A Type A broad scope licensee, for example, would use an RSC by the nature of its diverse program.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which of the following individuals is NOT a required member of the radiation safety committee (RSC)?

choices.text: An authorized user of each type of use permitted by the license
A representative of management who is neither an Authorized User (AU) nor an Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)

questions.explanation: The RSC must include: an AU of each type of use permitted by the license, the RSO, a representative of the nursing service, and a representative of management who is neither an AU nor an RSO. An Authorized Medical Physicist (AMP) is not a mandatory RSC member, though the committee may include other members the licensee considers appropriate. The nursing service representative is often overlooked but is explicitly required.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which of the following is within the authority and responsibilities of the radiation safety committee?

choices.text: Evaluating requests for a license application, renewal, or amendment before submission to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), and allowing an individual to work as an Authorized User (AU), Authorized Nuclear Pharmacist (ANP), or Authorized Medical Physicist (AMP)
Setting individual occupational dose limits for each radiation worker at the facility
Approving individual written directives for therapeutic administrations
Determining the frequency of radiation badge dosimetry review for all staff

questions.explanation: The Radiation Safety Committee (RSC) has authority and responsibilities for the radiation protection program including evaluating requests for a license application, renewal, or amendment before submission to the NRC, and allowing an individual to work as an AU, ANP, or AMP. Individual written directives are approved by the authorized user, not the committee. Occupational dose limits are set by regulation (not the RSC), and the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) oversees badge review frequency within the framework of the radiation protection program.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A Type A broad scope radioactive material (RAM) license is most likely held by which type of institution?

choices.text: A community hospital nuclear medicine department

questions.explanation: Type A licenses of broad scope are typically the largest licensed programs and encompass a broad range of uses. They use an Radiation Safety Committee (RSC), Radiation Safety Officer (RSO), and licensee-developed criteria. These licenses typically exist at large academic centers. Type B programs are smaller and less diverse, while Type C licenses are typically issued to institutions that do not need significant quantities of radioactive material but need flexibility - such as nuclear cardiology clinics or small research labs.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A Type C broad scope radioactive material (RAM) license is most appropriate for which type of institution?

choices.text: A hospital with a full nuclear medicine department performing both diagnostic and therapeutic procedures
A commercial nuclear pharmacy distributing radiopharmaceuticals to multiple facilities
A large academic center with diverse research and clinical programs
A nuclear cardiology clinic or small research lab requiring small quantities of a variety of radioactive materials

questions.explanation: Type C broad scope licensed programs are typically issued to institutions that do not require significant quantities of radioactive material but need the flexibility to possess a variety of different radioactive materials. Users are approved by the licensee based on training and experience criteria. These licenses usually exist for nuclear cardiology clinics or small research labs requiring small quantities of radioactive material.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: At what minimum frequency does the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) inspect Master Materials License (MML) holders?
questions.explanation: The NRC provides oversight of MML licensees and inspects MMLs at least every two years to evaluate how well the licensee is implementing their program. A Master Materials License is issued by the NRC to federal organizations authorizing use of byproduct material at multiple sites under federal agency jurisdiction. The MML allows the federal agency to conduct certain regulatory activities itself, including issuing permits, conducting inspections, and taking enforcement actions at its sites.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Do uptake, dilution, and excretion studies using unsealed byproduct material require a written directive?

choices.text: Yes, if the activity exceeds 1.11 MBq (30 µCi)
Yes, always, regardless of the activity administered
No, only if the material is obtained from a licensed manufacturer
No; a written directive is not required for uptake, dilution, and excretion studies

questions.explanation: Use of unsealed byproduct material for uptake, dilution, and excretion studies does not require a written directive. The licensee may use any unsealed byproduct material prepared for medical use for these studies if it is obtained from a licensed manufacturer, a positron emission tomography (PET) radioactive drug producer, or prepared by an Authorized Nuclear Pharmacist (ANP) or Authorized User (AU) with specific Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)-approved training. Radioactive Drug Research Committee (RDRC)-approved or Investigational New Drug (IND) byproduct material also does not require a written directive for these study types.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: An authorized user seeking to perform uptake, dilution, and excretion studies must complete how many total hours of training and experience, and what is the minimum number of classroom and laboratory hours?

choices.text: 60 total hours, minimum 8 classroom and laboratory hours
700 total hours, minimum 80 classroom and laboratory hours
80 total hours, minimum 8 classroom and laboratory hours

questions.explanation: The Authorized User (AU) of unsealed byproduct material for uptake, dilution, and excretion studies must complete 60 hours of training and experience in basic radionuclide handling techniques and radiation safety, including a minimum of 8 hours of classroom and laboratory training. This is significantly less than the requirements for imaging/localization studies (700 hours, 80 classroom/lab) or for use requiring a written directive (700 hours, 200 classroom hours).

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: An authorized user seeking to perform imaging and localization studies must complete how many total hours of training and experience, and what is the minimum number of classroom and laboratory hours?

choices.text: 700 total hours, minimum 80 classroom and laboratory hours
60 total hours, minimum 8 classroom and laboratory hours

questions.explanation: The Authorized User (AU) of unsealed byproduct material for imaging and localization studies must complete 700 hours of training and experience in basic radionuclide handling techniques and radiation safety, including a minimum of 80 hours of classroom and laboratory training. This is substantially more than the uptake/dilution/excretion AU requirement (60 hours, 8 classroom) and differs from the written directive AU requirement (700 hours, 200 classroom hours).

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: An authorized user seeking to use unsealed byproduct material for which a written directive is required must complete how many classroom hours as part of the 700-hour training requirement?
questions.explanation: For use of unsealed byproduct material requiring a written directive, the 700-hour training program must include 200 classroom hours. This is a higher classroom requirement than for imaging and localization studies (minimum 80 classroom hours out of 700), reflecting the additional complexity and risk associated with therapeutic administrations requiring written directives.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: To qualify as an authorized user for unsealed byproduct material requiring a written directive, a candidate must complete a minimum of how many supervised cases in each category for which Authorized User (AU) status is sought?
questions.explanation: Work experience must involve a minimum of three cases in each of the relevant categories for which the individual is requesting AU status. The required categories include: oral administration of less than or equal to 33 mCi (1.22 GBq) of sodium iodide 131I; oral administration of greater than 33 mCi of sodium iodide 131I; and parenteral administration of any radioactive drug primarily used for electron emission, beta, alpha radiation, or photon energy less than 150 keV, when a written directive is required.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A written directive is required for oral administration of sodium iodide 131I at what activity threshold?
questions.explanation: A written directive dated and signed by an authorized user is required for the oral administration of all 131I quantities greater than 1.11 MBq (30 µCi). The 1.22 GBq (33 mCi) threshold is significant for a different reason: it distinguishes the two training tiers for AUs performing 131I therapy. But the written directive threshold itself is the much lower value of 30 µCi (1.11 MBq).

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A negative serum beta-hCG pregnancy test must be documented before therapeutic radiopharmaceutical administration in which patient population?

choices.text: All female patients of any age
All female patients under 65 years old who have not had a hysterectomy
All patients requiring a written directive, regardless of sex or age
All potentially childbearing individuals under 50 years old

questions.explanation: A negative serum beta-hCG pregnancy test must be documented in the patient's chart for all potentially childbearing individuals who are under 50 years old when receiving therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals. The pregnancy test must be within one week of the 131I sodium iodide therapy. A pregnancy test is not necessary if the patient has had a remote bilateral tubal ligation or hysterectomy.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: The pre-therapy pregnancy test for a patient receiving therapeutic sodium iodide 131I must be performed within what time frame before treatment?
questions.explanation: The pregnancy test must be within one week of the sodium iodide 131I therapy. This requirement applies to potentially childbearing individuals under 50 years old. A pregnancy test is not required if the patient has had a remote bilateral tubal ligation or hysterectomy, as these procedures eliminate the possibility of pregnancy.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: When a private room is unavailable for an inpatient receiving 131I therapy, with which type of patient may the 131I patient be housed?

choices.text: A patient in a double room who is immunocompromised and requires isolation
Any patient who has received informed consent and agrees to share the room
Another patient who has also received therapy with unsealed byproduct material and who also cannot be released
Any patient in a private room on the same floor

questions.explanation: For each patient receiving therapy with unsealed byproduct material who cannot be released, the licensee must quarter the patient either in a private room with a private sanitary facility or with another individual who has also received therapy with unsealed byproduct material and who also cannot be released. This provision ensures that roommates are not general-population patients who would face unexpected radiation exposure.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: What signage must be placed on the door of an inpatient room before a patient receives therapeutic 131I?

choices.text: A standard radiation caution symbol only
A restricted access sign requiring Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) authorization for entry
A "Radioactive Materials" sign indicating the type of isotope and activity administered
Radiation hazard signage and a "no housekeeping services" notice

questions.explanation: Before a patient is dosed, the room should be prepared with signage indicating a radiation hazard and "no housekeeping services" placed on the door. The licensee must also visibly post the room with a "Radioactive Materials" sign and include a note on the door or in the chart specifying where and how long visitors may stay. Linen and trash hampers are placed inside the room, and frequently touched surfaces are wrapped in plastic.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which surfaces in the inpatient 131I therapy room should be wrapped in plastic before treatment?

choices.text: Surfaces the patient may frequently touch, such as the toilet, faucet handles, phone, and bedrails
Only the bed, because it is the primary source of patient contact
All horizontal surfaces in the room
The floor and window sills only

questions.explanation: All surfaces the patient may frequently touch should be wrapped in plastic before the patient is dosed. These include the toilet, faucet handles, phone, and bedrails. Materials used in the care of the patient are left in the room for the entire hospital stay. Wrapping high-contact surfaces with plastic reduces the risk of surface contamination and facilitates decontamination after discharge.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Male inpatients receiving 131I therapy are specifically instructed to do which of the following regarding voiding?

choices.text: Wear disposable protective clothing while using the restroom
Use a urinal rather than the toilet
Collect and measure all urine output for radioactivity monitoring

questions.explanation: Male patients receiving 131I should be instructed to sit while voiding. All patients - male and female - should be instructed to flush the toilet twice with the lid closed to reduce the risk of aerosolization of 131I-containing urine. Vigorous hydration is highly encouraged because it hastens the biologic elimination of iodine. Hospitals may also ask patients to handle their own urine collection so staff avoid close contact with the radioactive fluid.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Why is vigorous hydration encouraged for inpatients receiving therapeutic sodium iodide 131I?

choices.text: It reduces the concentration of iodine in the thyroid gland
It reduces the absorbed dose to the salivary glands
It prevents nephrotoxicity associated with high-dose iodine administration
It hastens biologic elimination of the radiopharmaceutical

questions.explanation: Vigorous hydration is highly encouraged because it hastens biologic elimination of 131I from the body. Faster excretion shortens the duration of whole-body radiation exposure to the patient and reduces contamination from radioactive body fluids. Encouraging frequent showers for the first two weeks after treatment (because sweat is a source of contamination) addresses a similar radiation protection goal.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: For the first two weeks after 131I therapy, patients are encouraged to take frequent showers. What is the radiation safety rationale for this?

choices.text: Showering reduces dermal uptake of iodine-131 from the environment
Sweat is a source of contamination, and showering reduces surface contamination
Showering accelerates the biologic half-life of iodine-131
Showering reduces the dose rate at 1 meter by removing surface-deposited radioiodine

questions.explanation: Patients are encouraged to take frequent showers as tolerated for the first two weeks after 131I treatment because sweat is a source of contamination. Radioiodine is excreted through sweat as well as urine, and residual contamination on the skin contributes to surface contamination of the patient's environment. Showering thus serves as a simple decontamination measure.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which visitor categories are prohibited from entering the room of an inpatient receiving 131I therapy?

choices.text: Unvaccinated visitors and visitors with chronic illness
Pregnant visitors and visitors younger than 18 years
Non-family visitors and visitors from outside the immediate household
Visitors over 65 years old and children under 12

questions.explanation: Visitor safety is promoted by prohibiting pregnant visitors and visitors younger than 18 years from the room of an inpatient receiving 131I therapy. Both pregnant individuals and minors are at increased radiation sensitivity. State regulations and hospital policies vary, but visits for permitted visitors are typically limited to 30 minutes and require that visitors maintain a distance of at least 6 feet from the patient.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: What are the typical time and distance restrictions for permitted visitors to an inpatient receiving 131I therapy?

choices.text: No more than 15 minutes, at least 3 feet from the patient
No more than 60 minutes, at least 3 feet from the patient
No more than 30 minutes, at least 10 feet from the patient
No more than 30 minutes, at least 6 feet from the patient

questions.explanation: While state regulations and hospital policies vary, visits to inpatients receiving 131I are typically limited to 30 minutes and require that visitors maintain a distance of at least 6 feet from the patient. These two restrictions together - limiting time and maximizing distance - apply the principles of as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA) to visitor exposure management.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Surveys of an inpatient 131I therapy room should be performed at what minimum frequency?
questions.explanation: The patient and room should be surveyed with dosimeters at prescribed points at least daily. Survey points include: 1 meter from the patient's chest, each side of the bed, the foot of the bed, the doorway, the visitor chair, the inside and outside of the door, and the adjacent patient wall. The daily minimum frequency ensures timely detection of changing dose rates as the patient's activity decreases over time.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: When is an inpatient receiving 131I therapy generally considered safe for discharge?

choices.text: When the patient's urine radioactivity falls below 1 µCi per 24-hour collection
When the dose rate at 30 cm from the patient is less than 5 mrem/hr
When 72 hours have elapsed since administration, regardless of dose rate
When the dose rate at 1 meter from the patient's chest is 7 mrem/hr or less

questions.explanation: When survey readings at 1 meter from the patient's chest are 7 mrem/hr or less, the patient is considered generally safe for discharge. This threshold corresponds to the release criterion in the regulatory table - a dose rate at 1 meter of 0.07 mSv/hr (7 mrem/hr) for 131I - which is the level below which third-party dose is unlikely to exceed 500 mrem. The discharge criteria may vary from state to state and facility to facility.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Under Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) regulations, a 131I therapy patient treated as an outpatient may be released when the radiation dose to third parties is not likely to exceed what level?
questions.explanation: NRC regulations allow 131I therapy patients to be released following treatment when the radiation dose to third parties is not likely to exceed 500 mrem (5 mSv). The regulations assume this dose would principally apply to the patient's family or other caregivers during the first few days at home. Treating physicians must consider the patient's living conditions and provide instructions for avoiding unnecessary exposure to others.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Where does the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) stand on the practice of recommending that outpatient 131I therapy patients stay at a hotel immediately after treatment?

choices.text: The NRC requires licensees to offer this option to all outpatient 131I recipients
The NRC strongly discourages medical licensees from recommending that patients stay at hotels immediately after treatment
The NRC endorses this practice as it protects the patient's household contacts
The NRC has no position on hotel stays as long as doses to third parties remain below 500 mrem

questions.explanation: The NRC strongly discourages medical licensees who conduct outpatient 131I treatment from recommending patients stay at hotels immediately after treatment. The concern is that hotels expose members of the general public to radiation from other guests sharing rooms, hallways, or lobbies. The NRC also reminds treating physicians to inquire about the patient's intended destination so appropriate instructions can be given.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A licensee must provide written instructions to a released patient when the total effective dose equivalent to any other individual from exposure to the released patient is likely to exceed what level?
questions.explanation: The licensee must provide the released individual with instructions, including written instructions, on actions recommended to maintain doses to other individuals as low as reasonably achievable if the total effective dose equivalent to any other individual is likely to exceed 1 millisievert (0.1 rem). This threshold is lower than the 5 mSv (0.5 rem) release criterion - written instructions are required before that outer limit is reached.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: According to the patient release table, what is the maximum activity of 131I at or below which a patient may be released without documentation of retained activity?
questions.explanation: The release table specifies that a patient administered 131I may be released if the activity at the time of release is at or below 33 mCi (1.2 GBq), or if the dose rate at 1 meter is at or below 7 mrem/hr (0.07 mSv/hr). The 9 mCi value corresponds to 125I implants, and 64 mCi corresponds to 111In. The 33 mCi threshold for 131I also coincides with the activity that defines the two Authorized User (AU) training tiers for therapeutic 131I administration.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Why are there no established activity or dose rate thresholds governing the outpatient release of patients administered 90Y?

choices.text: All 90Y therapies require inpatient admission, so outpatient release criteria do not apply
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has not yet established release criteria for 90Y and is awaiting further study
90Y is restricted to inpatient administration only and is never released
Activity and dose rate limits are not applicable because of the minimal exposures to members of the public from activities normally administered

questions.explanation: No activity or dose rate thresholds are established for 90Y because the exposures to members of the public resulting from activities normally administered for diagnostic or therapeutic purposes are minimal. 90Y is a pure beta emitter with very limited external dose contribution at distance, so standard release thresholds do not apply in the same way as for gamma-emitting radionuclides. 90Y patients are routinely released; the NRC simply does not set numeric activity or dose rate limits for this isotope.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: How must licensed radioactive materials in a nuclear medicine facility be secured?

choices.text: In a double-locked container with an independent log of access
Either by storage in a locked room or by constant surveillance
In a lead-lined safe accessible only to authorized users
Under direct Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) supervision at all times

questions.explanation: Licensed materials must be secured either by storage in a locked room (such as the nuclear pharmacy or "hot lab") or by constant surveillance (such as in imaging rooms where patient dosages may be located during use). The two acceptable methods reflect the practical reality that materials in active use cannot always be locked away, but must at minimum be under continuous observation.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A dose calibrator in the hot lab should ideally be placed behind which type of shielding?

choices.text: Concrete shielding with a 1-foot minimum thickness
Tungsten shielding for optimal attenuation efficiency

questions.explanation: The dose calibrator is often placed behind a lead or leaded-glass shield to minimize radiation exposure to the individual while working with radioactivity. Patient dosages and shielded vials are also generally placed and/or stored behind this shield. Leaded glass allows visual monitoring of calibration activity while still attenuating gamma radiation.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Radiation safety instruction for personnel caring for patients who cannot be released must be provided at what frequency?

choices.text: Quarterly, coinciding with Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) badge reading reviews
Once at hire, and then only if procedures change significantly

questions.explanation: A licensee must provide radiation safety instruction initially and at least annually to personnel caring for patients or human research subjects who cannot be released. The instruction must cover patient control, visitor control (including routine visitation to hospitalized individuals), contamination and waste control, and notification of the RSO and Authorized User (AU) in the event of a medical emergency or patient death. Records of individuals receiving instruction must be retained.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which of the following topics must be included in the required radiation safety instruction for personnel caring for patients who cannot be released?

choices.text: A review of the facility's radioactive material (RAM) license conditions and authorized activities
The complete sequence of the major spill procedure from Table 8
Contamination and waste control, and notification of the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) or designee and Authorized User (AU) if the patient has a medical emergency or dies
Annual review of each staff member's personal dosimetry results

questions.explanation: The required instruction must cover: patient or human research subject control; visitor control, including routine visitation to hospitalized individuals; contamination and waste control; and notification of the RSO (or their designee) and an AU if the patient or human research subject has a medical emergency or dies. RAM license conditions and personal dosimetry results are not listed as required topics for this specific instruction requirement.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: If a patient receiving inpatient 131I therapy has a medical emergency, who must be notified as soon as possible?

choices.text: The authorized user only; RSO involvement is not required for medical emergencies
The RSO only; the authorized user is notified at the next Radiation Safety Committee (RSC) meeting
The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) (or designee) and the authorized user
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) Operations Center and the hospital administrator

questions.explanation: The licensee must notify the RSO (or their designee) and the authorized user as soon as possible if the patient or human research subject has a medical emergency or dies. Both parties must be notified - the RSO to manage radiation safety aspects of the emergency, and the Authorized User (AU) as the responsible physician for the patient's medical care and the administered radioactive material. The regulations specify both the RSO and AU, not one or the other.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: What is the maximum permissible concentration of 99Mo in a 99mTc eluate that may be administered to humans?
questions.explanation: A licensee may not administer to humans a radiopharmaceutical that contains more than 0.15 kBq of 99Mo per MBq of 99mTc (equivalent to 0.15 µCi of 99Mo per mCi of 99mTc). Exceeding this breakthrough limit must be reported by telephone within 7 calendar days of discovery and in writing to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) within 30 calendar days. The 99Mo limit reflects the high-energy gamma and beta emissions of 99Mo, which would deliver unanticipated radiation dose to the patient.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: What is the maximum permissible concentration of 82Sr in a 82Rb chloride injection that may be administered to humans?

choices.text: 0.02 kBq of 82Sr per MBq of 82Rb chloride
0.2 kBq of 82Sr per MBq of 82Rb chloride
0.15 kBq of 82Sr per MBq of 82Rb chloride
1.0 kBq of 82Sr per MBq of 82Rb chloride

questions.explanation: A licensee may not administer to humans a radiopharmaceutical that contains more than 0.02 kBq of 82Sr per MBq of 82Rb chloride injection (0.02 µCi of 82Sr per mCi of 82Rb). This is distinct from the 85Sr limit (0.2 kBq per MBq of 82Rb), which is ten times higher. Both strontium isotopes must be monitored before the first patient of the day when using a 82Sr/82Rb generator.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: What is the maximum permissible concentration of 85Sr in a 82Rb chloride injection that may be administered to humans?
questions.explanation: A licensee may not administer to humans a radiopharmaceutical containing more than 0.2 kBq of 85Sr per MBq of 82Rb chloride injection. This is ten times the 82Sr limit (0.02 kBq/MBq). For 82Sr/82Rb generators, the concentrations of both 82Sr and 85Sr must be measured before the first patient of the day - not just at the time of elution - to ensure compliance.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: For a 82Sr/82Rb generator, when must the concentrations of 82Sr and 85Sr be measured to ensure compliance with permissible limits?

choices.text: At the time of each individual generator elution
After every fifth patient of the day
Before the first patient of the day
At the end of each day of use

questions.explanation: For 82Sr/82Rb generators, the concentration of radionuclides 82Sr and 85Sr must be measured before the first patient of the day. This daily pre-use measurement ensures breakthrough concentrations are within permissible limits before any patient receives the 82Rb radiopharmaceutical. The eluates from each generator should also be measured to demonstrate compliance, but the specific daily timing requirement applies to the strontium breakthrough measurement.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A licensee discovers that a 99mTc eluate exceeded the permissible 99Mo concentration. By when must the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) be notified by telephone?
questions.explanation: The licensee must report by telephone any measurement - within 7 calendar days after discovery - that indicates an eluate exceeded the permissible concentration. A separate written report to the NRC must also be submitted within 30 calendar days after discovery. Both the telephone notification and the written report are required; the 7-day telephone deadline is distinct from the 30-day written report deadline.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A written report to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) after a generator eluate exceeds permissible breakthrough concentrations must be submitted within what time frame?
questions.explanation: The written report must be submitted to the NRC within 30 calendar days after discovery of an eluate that exceeded permissible concentration at the time of generator elution. The telephone report must be made within 7 calendar days. The written report must include: the action taken; the patient dose assessment; the methodology used if the eluate was administered to a person; and the probable cause and assessment of any failure in equipment, procedures, or training that contributed to the excessive readings.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Unlike 99Mo/99mTc and 82Sr/82Rb generators, the 68Ge/68Ga generator has which of the following characteristics regarding breakthrough limits?

choices.text: It is exempt from breakthrough monitoring because 68Ge decays to a non-radioactive daughter
It has a more stringent breakthrough limit than 99Mo/99mTc due to 68Ge's longer half-life
No specific breakthrough limit is established; applicants must individually commit to safety protocols with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
Its breakthrough limit is the same as the 99Mo limit (0.15 kBq per MBq of product)

questions.explanation: No specific breakthrough limit is specified for 68Ge/68Ga generators, unlike the established limits for 99Mo/99mTc and 82Sr/82Rb systems. Applicants using 68Ge/68Ga generators must individually commit to safety protocols to the NRC. This distinction is notable because 68Ge breakthrough could lead to contamination of the 68Ga radiopharmaceutical, potentially causing unnecessary radiation exposure to patients. 68Ge has a long half-life (271 days), which makes breakthrough particularly concerning.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Records of authority and responsibilities for radiation protection programs - including Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) and program changes - must be retained for how long?
questions.explanation: A licensee must retain records of actions related to RSO designation and radiation program changes for 5 years. The record must include a summary of the actions taken and a signature of licensee management, and must include copies of previous and current radiation safety procedures. This 5-year retention period is notable because virtually all other records in this section - written directives, instrument calibrations, dosage determinations, leak tests, and surveys - have a 3-year retention period.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A licensee shall retain a copy of each written directive for how long?

choices.text: Indefinitely, as long as the relevant radiopharmaceuticals remain in use

questions.explanation: A licensee must retain a copy of each written directive for 3 years. This 3-year retention period is consistent with the retention periods for instrument calibrations, dosage determinations, leak tests and inventory records, and survey records. The single exception among commonly retained records is the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)/authority change record, which must be kept for 5 years.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which of the following must be included in a record of dosage determination for unsealed byproduct material?

choices.text: The dose calibrator model and the results of the most recent calibration
The radiopharmaceutical, patient name or ID, prescribed dosage, determined dosage with date and time, and name of the person who determined the dosage
The lot number and expiration date of the radiopharmaceutical, and the room where administration occurred
The patient's insurance information and referring physician's signature

questions.explanation: The dosage determination record must contain: the radiopharmaceutical; the patient's name or identification number; the prescribed dosage; the determined dosage including date and time (or a notation that the total activity is less than 1.1 MBq/30 µCi); and the name of the person who determined the dosage. Patient insurance information, referring physician signature, room location, and dose calibrator calibration details are not required elements of the dosage record, though calibration records are separately maintained.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Records of leak tests and inventory of sealed sources must be retained for how long?

choices.text: The lifetime of the sealed source
1 year after the source is removed from service

questions.explanation: A licensee must retain records of leak tests for 3 years. These records must include the model and serial number of the source (if assigned), the identity of each source by radionuclide and its estimated activity, the results of the test, and the name of the person who performed it. The licensee must also retain records of the semi-annual physical inventory of sealed sources and brachytherapy sources for 3 years.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: What information must be included in a record of a radiation area survey?

choices.text: The date of the survey, results, instrument used, and name of the person who performed it
The regulatory limit for each area surveyed and the percentage of that limit measured
The date, results, instrument used, and signatures of both the surveyor and the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)
The date, results, instrument model only (serial number not required)

questions.explanation: Survey records must include: the date of the survey; the results; the instrument used to make the survey; and the name of the person who performed it. RSO co-signature is not required for routine survey records. The serial number of the instrument is a required element of instrument calibration records (not survey records), and regulatory limit comparisons are not a required record element.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: A licensee discovers that licensed radioactive material has been lost or stolen, and there is a possibility that persons in unrestricted areas could be exposed. What immediate action is required?

choices.text: File a written report with the NRC within 30 days; telephone notification is optional
Notify the local law enforcement agency and await NRC guidance before filing a report
Report by telephone to the NRC, followed by a written report within 30 days of the telephone report
Submit a written report to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) within 15 days

questions.explanation: Each licensee must report by telephone to the NRC any lost, stolen, or missing licensed material that could result in exposure to persons in unrestricted areas. A written report must then be submitted within 30 days after making the telephone report. The written report must include: a description of the material (kind, quantity, and chemical/physical form); circumstances of the loss or theft; disposition or probable disposition; exposures of individuals; actions taken or planned for recovery; and procedures adopted to prevent recurrence.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Within how many days must a licensee submit a written report after discovering that a radiation worker has received a dose in excess of any applicable occupational dose limit?
questions.explanation: Each licensee must submit a written report within 30 days after learning of doses in excess of any of the occupational dose limits for adults or minors, the limits for an embryo/fetus of a declared pregnant individual, or the limits for an individual member of the public. A similar 30-day written report is required for excessive radiation air emissions, excessive radiation in a restricted space, or 10 times the limits of an unrestricted area.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: For individuals who have been occupationally overexposed, what specific personal information must be included in the written dose exceedance report and labeled for privacy?

choices.text: The individual's name and supervisor's name, labeled as confidential personnel information
The individual's medical history and pre-employment radiation dose summary
The individual's name, Social Security account number, and date of birth, clearly labeled as "Privacy Act Information: Not for Public Disclosure"
The individual's employee ID number and department name

questions.explanation: For reports involving occupationally overexposed individuals, the report must include the individual's name, Social Security account number, and date of birth, clearly labeled with "Privacy Act Information: Not for Public Disclosure." This privacy designation protects the individual's sensitive identifying information from general public disclosure while still meeting the regulatory requirement to inform the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) of the overexposure event.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: At or below what activity may a patient who received 64Cu be released without exceeding dose limits to members of the public?
questions.explanation: The patient release table specifies that a patient administered 64Cu may be released if the activity at the time of release is at or below 230 mCi (8.4 GBq), or if the dose rate at 1 meter is at or below 27 mrem/hr (0.27 mSv/hr). The 33 mCi threshold applies to 131I, the 64 mCi threshold applies to 111In, and 160 mCi applies to 123I.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: At or below what activity may a patient who received 123I be released without exceeding dose limits to members of the public?
questions.explanation: The patient release table specifies that a patient administered 123I may be released if the activity at the time of release is at or below 160 mCi (6.0 GBq), or if the dose rate at 1 meter is at or below 26 mrem/hr (0.26 mSv/hr). The 64 mCi threshold applies to 111In, 230 mCi applies to 64Cu, and 430 mCi applies to 201Tl.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: At or below what activity may a patient who received 99mTc be released without exceeding dose limits to members of the public?
questions.explanation: The patient release table specifies that a patient administered 99mTc may be released if the activity at the time of release is at or below 760 mCi (28 GBq), or if the dose rate at 1 meter is at or below 58 mrem/hr (0.58 mSv/hr). The 160 mCi threshold applies to 123I, 430 mCi applies to 201Tl, and 1,200 mCi is not a listed threshold in the table.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: When the projected dose to a breastfeeding infant or child could exceed 1 mSv (0.1 rem) assuming no interruption of breastfeeding, what must the release instructions include in addition to standard written instructions?

choices.text: A mandatory 24-hour hold before the patient is permitted to breastfeed
A written directive signed by the authorized user and the patient
Documentation that the patient has been counseled by a board-certified lactation consultant
Guidance on interruption or discontinuation of breastfeeding, and information on the potential consequences of failing to follow that guidance

questions.explanation: When the projected dose to a breastfeeding infant or child could exceed 1 mSv (0.1 rem) - assuming no interruption of breastfeeding - the release instructions must additionally include: (1) guidance on the interruption or discontinuation of breastfeeding, and (2) information on the potential consequences of failure to follow the guidance. The other choices describe requirements that do not exist under the applicable regulations.

questions.chapterName: Section 6: Administrative/Practice Regulations, Responsibilities and Training
questions.stem: Which of the following situations would NOT require a licensee to maintain a 3-year record of the basis for authorizing a patient's release?

choices.text: The TEDE was calculated using an occupancy factor of less than 0.25 at 1 meter
The TEDE was calculated accounting for self-shielding by tissue
The patient's measured activity at the time of release was at or below the standard regulatory threshold
The total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) was calculated using the retained activity rather than the activity administered
The TEDE was calculated using the biological or effective half-life

questions.explanation: A 3-year record is required when the TEDE is calculated using any of four specific methods: (1) retained activity rather than activity administered, (2) occupancy factor less than 0.25 at 1 meter, (3) biological or effective half-life, or (4) self-shielding by tissue. Answers B, A, D, and E each describe one of these four triggering conditions. Simply releasing a patient whose activity at the time of release is at or below the standard regulatory threshold - the most straightforward release scenario - does not trigger the documentation requirement.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: For an incident to qualify as a medical event under Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) regulations, which of the following must be true?

choices.text: The dose difference alone determines whether an event qualifies, regardless of how it occurred
Both a specified dose threshold is exceeded AND a qualifying administration error occurs
Either a specified dose threshold is exceeded OR an administration error occurs - either condition alone is sufficient
An administration error alone - such as wrong drug or wrong patient - is automatically reportable regardless of dose

questions.explanation: A medical event requires that BOTH conditions are simultaneously met. Condition 1 is a dose difference from the prescribed dose or expected dose exceeding one of three thresholds: more than 5 rem (0.05 Sv) effective dose equivalent, more than 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to an organ or tissue, or more than 50 rem (0.5 Sv) shallow dose equivalent to the skin. Condition 2 is the occurrence of one of several qualifying administration errors (dosage off by 20% or more, wrong drug, wrong route, wrong patient, wrong body part with 50% or more excess dose, or a sealed source leak). Neither condition alone is sufficient.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A dose difference between the administered and prescribed dosage that exceeds which threshold satisfies the effective dose equivalent criterion for a medical event?
questions.explanation: The effective dose equivalent criterion requires that the administered dosage result in an effective dose equivalent (EDE) that differs from the prescribed dose by more than 5 rem (0.05 Sv). This is a lower threshold than the organ/tissue or skin thresholds, both of which are 50 rem (0.5 Sv). The 1 rem value corresponds to the occupational total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) limit for declared pregnant workers, and 50 rem is the organ/tissue or skin dose threshold for the same medical event definition.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: What dose difference to an organ or tissue - above the dose that would have resulted from the prescribed dosage - is required to satisfy the dose criterion for a medical event?
questions.explanation: The organ or tissue dose criterion requires that the delivered dose differ from the prescribed dose by more than 50 rem (0.5 Sv). The same 50 rem threshold applies to the shallow dose equivalent to the skin. The effective dose equivalent (EDE) threshold is lower, at 5 rem (0.05 Sv). The 20 rem value does not appear in the medical event definition.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A dosage that differs from the prescribed dosage by at least what percentage qualifies as an administration incident for the purpose of medical event reporting?
questions.explanation: A dosage that differs from the prescribed dosage by 20% or more - whether too high or too low - satisfies the administration incident criterion. This 20% threshold must be met in conjunction with one of the three dose difference thresholds; the percentage difference alone is not sufficient to constitute a medical event.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A patient undergoing 131I therapy receives a dosage that is 24% higher than prescribed. The resulting increase in effective dose equivalent above what the prescribed dosage would have yielded is 4.2 rem. Does this constitute a medical event?

choices.text: Yes - the dosage deviation exceeds 20%, satisfying the administration incident criterion
No - 131I therapy is exempt from the medical event dose thresholds
No - the dose difference does not exceed the 5 rem effective dose equivalent (EDE) threshold required for a medical event
Yes - any unauthorized increase in 131I dosage requires reporting to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)

questions.explanation: A medical event requires that BOTH conditions be met. Here, Condition 2 is met (dosage differs by more than 20%), but Condition 1 is not - the EDE difference of 4.2 rem does not exceed the required 5 rem threshold. Because both conditions must be satisfied simultaneously, this does not qualify as a medical event. Answer A correctly identifies that the dosage deviation criterion is met but incorrectly concludes this alone is sufficient.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A patient receives the correct radiopharmaceutical by the correct route to the correct patient and body part. Due to a calibration error, the dosage administered is 18% below the prescribed amount, resulting in an effective dose equivalent (EDE) difference of 9 rem below what the prescribed dosage would have yielded. Is this a medical event?

choices.text: No - underdosing does not qualify as a medical event under any circumstances
No - the dosage deviation does not reach the 20% threshold required for the administration incident criterion
Yes - the dose difference exceeds 5 rem EDE, satisfying the dose criterion
Yes - underdosing carries the same reporting obligation as overdosing

questions.explanation: Although the dose difference (9 rem) exceeds the 5 rem EDE threshold, the dosage deviation (18%) does not meet the 20% threshold required for the administration incident criterion. Because both conditions must be met and Condition 2 is not satisfied here, this is not a medical event. Answer B is incorrect - underdosing can constitute a medical event if both conditions are met (i.e., if the dosage were also off by 20% or more).

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A patient receives the wrong radiopharmaceutical. The resulting effective dose equivalent to the patient is 8 rem above what the prescribed dosage would have yielded. Is this a medical event?

choices.text: Yes - any administration of the wrong drug is automatically a medical event regardless of dose
No - wrong-drug errors are only reportable when the dose difference exceeds 50 rem to an organ
No - only wrong-route errors combined with dose threshold exceedances qualify as medical events
Yes - administration of the wrong drug together with a dose difference exceeding 5 rem effective dose equivalent (EDE) satisfies both required conditions

questions.explanation: Both conditions for a medical event are met. Condition 1 is satisfied because the EDE difference (8 rem) exceeds the 5 rem threshold. Condition 2 is satisfied because the wrong drug was administered. Answer A is incorrect - the dose criterion must also be met. Answer B is incorrect - the 50 rem threshold applies to organ/tissue dose, not EDE, and a dose difference exceeding 5 rem EDE is sufficient.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Administration of a radiopharmaceutical to the wrong part of the body qualifies as an administration incident only if the dose to that body part exceeds the intended dose by at least what percentage?
questions.explanation: The wrong-body-part criterion requires that the unintended body part receive a dose that exceeds - by 50% or more - the dose that area should have received. The 20% threshold applies to the general dosage deviation criterion (too high or too low from the prescribed dosage), not to wrong-body-part errors.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: The decision to implement a major versus minor spill procedure depends on several incident-specific variables. Which of the following is NOT one of those variables?

choices.text: The radiotoxicity of the spilled material
The time elapsed since the radiopharmaceutical was prepared
The likelihood of contamination spread and the types of surfaces contaminated
The number of individuals affected by the spill

questions.explanation: The factors that determine whether a major or minor spill procedure is used include the number of individuals affected, other hazards present, likelihood of contamination spread, the types of surfaces contaminated, and the radiotoxicity of the spilled material. The time since preparation - which affects residual activity - may influence the approach taken but is not listed among the formal decision variables. For some spills of short-lived radionuclides, restricted access pending complete decay may actually be the best procedure.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: What is the threshold activity at or above which a spill of 131I is classified as a major spill?
questions.explanation: Spills of 131I are classified as major at 1 mCi or greater, and minor below 1 mCi. The same 1 mCi threshold applies to 90Y. The 2 mCi threshold applies to 177Lu, and 10 mCi applies to isotopes such as 67Ga, 111In, and 123I.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A 3 mCi spill of 177Lu occurs in a nuclear medicine preparation area. Which spill classification applies?

choices.text: Minor spill - handle per minor spill protocol
Major spill - follow major spill procedures and notify Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)
No formal spill classification applies to 177Lu

questions.explanation: The major spill threshold for 177Lu is 2 mCi. A 3 mCi spill exceeds this threshold and is therefore classified as a major spill, requiring implementation of major spill procedures, including clearing the area, covering (not cleaning) the spill, shielding if safe to do so, securing the room, and notifying the RSO. No evacuation level is established for 177Lu.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A spill of 300 mCi of 18F occurs in a positron emission tomography (PET) radiopharmacy. Which response is required?

choices.text: No response required - 18F decays rapidly and poses no significant contamination risk
Evacuation of the area is required
Major spill - clear the area, cover the spill, and notify the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)
Minor spill - the technologist may clean up per minor spill protocol

questions.explanation: The evacuation threshold for 18F is 250 mCi. A spill of 300 mCi exceeds this threshold, requiring area evacuation in addition to major spill procedures. The major spill threshold for 18F is also 100 mCi, so this would be a major spill regardless, but the 300 mCi level additionally triggers the evacuation requirement.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A 12 mCi spill of 123I occurs. Which response is correct?

choices.text: Minor spill protocol - clean up immediately using gloves and absorbent paper
Major spill protocol - cover, do not clean, clear the area, and notify Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)
Restricted access pending decay is preferred due to 123I's short half-life
Evacuation of the area is required

questions.explanation: The major spill threshold for 123I is 10 mCi. A 12 mCi spill exceeds this threshold and requires major spill procedures: notify persons to leave, cover (do not clean) the spill, shield the source if safely possible, secure the room, and notify the RSO. The evacuation threshold for 123I is 15 mCi; since 12 mCi does not reach that level, area evacuation is not required. Answer C is incorrect - restricted access pending decay may be appropriate for some short-lived isotopes, but 123I has a 13-hour half-life and a 12 mCi spill requires active major spill response.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: For which of the following radionuclides would any amount spilled be classified as a major spill, with no minor spill threshold?
questions.explanation: For 223Ra, 225Ac, and 212Pb, any spill - regardless of amount - is classified as a major spill; no minor spill threshold exists for these isotopes. In contrast, 131I has a minor/major dividing line at 1 mCi, 90Y at 1 mCi, and 68Ga at 20 mCi.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: In the event of a major radioactive spill, which of the following actions should NOT be performed?

choices.text: Covering the spill with absorbent paper to prevent spread
Locking or otherwise securing the area to prevent entry
Removing contaminated clothing and flushing contaminated skin
Immediately cleaning up the spill using disposable gloves and absorbent paper

questions.explanation: In a major spill, the contaminated area should be covered to prevent spread, but cleanup should NOT be attempted by those on site. The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) must be notified, and the RSO will supervise the cleanup and complete the required reports. Immediate self-initiated cleanup is the appropriate response to a minor spill, not a major one. Covering the spill (A), securing the area (C), and personnel decontamination (D) are all correct steps in the major spill protocol.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: During major spill personnel decontamination, if contamination persists on the skin after washing with mild soap and water, what additional step should be taken?

choices.text: Apply a chelating agent and contact poison control
Cover the area with plastic to induce perspiration, then wash again
Refer the individual to a nuclear medicine physician for internal dosimetry assessment
Apply an iodine-based antiseptic to bind the radioactive material

questions.explanation: If contamination remains after the initial wash, the area should be covered with plastic to induce perspiration, then washed again to remove any contamination released by the perspiration. This is the described technique for persistent skin contamination following a major spill. Chelating agents and other interventions are not specified in this context.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Which of the following most accurately describes the correct response to a minor radioactive spill?

choices.text: Clear the area of all personnel, cover the spill, lock the room, and call the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO)
Notify persons in the area, cover the spill, then clean it up using gloves and absorbent paper; survey afterward and report to RSO
Immediately evacuate the building and contact the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) emergency line
Restrict access to the area and wait for the RSO to arrive before taking any action

questions.explanation: The minor spill procedure involves: notifying persons in the area, covering the spill with absorbent paper, then cleaning it up using disposable gloves and absorbent paper (folding the paper with the clean side out and placing it in a labeled bag), surveying the area and personnel afterward, reporting to the RSO, and completing the spill documentation. This contrasts with the major spill procedure, in which the area is covered but NOT cleaned, personnel are cleared, the room is secured, and the RSO handles cleanup.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
