questions.stem: When cleaning up a minor radioactive spill, how should the contaminated absorbent paper be folded before disposal?

choices.text: Rolled tightly and placed loose in a standard waste bin
With the clean side out, to minimize surface contamination of the bag and hands
With the contaminated side facing out, to allow radiation monitoring of the package
Folded flat and sealed with radiation hazard tape

questions.explanation: The contaminated absorbent paper should be carefully folded with the clean side out before placing it in a labeled plastic bag for transfer to a radioactive waste container. Folding clean side out minimizes the risk of additional contamination to hands, gloves, and the outside of the bag during handling.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: For which radionuclide does any amount released as a gas require immediate evacuation of the area?
questions.explanation: 133Xe is a radioactive gas; any detectable release requires evacuation of the area. Unlike the other isotopes listed, 133Xe has no minor or major spill classification - only an evacuate designation for any amount. 131I and 90Y have a 1 mCi minor/major threshold, and 18F evacuates at 250 mCi.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: What is the maximum allowable removable surface contamination for 131I in a restricted area?
questions.explanation: The allowable surface contamination limit for 131I - along with 111In, 123I, 177Lu, and 90Y - is 2,000 dpm per 100 cm2 of surface area. The 200 dpm/100 cm2 limit applies to all alpha emitters, and the 20,000 dpm/100 cm2 limit applies to 67Ga, 99mTc, and 201Tl.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: What is the maximum allowable removable surface contamination for 99mTc in a restricted area?
questions.explanation: The allowable surface contamination limit for 99mTc - along with 67Ga and 201Tl - is 20,000 dpm per 100 cm2. This is a less restrictive limit than the 2,000 dpm/100 cm2 that applies to isotopes such as 131I, 123I, 111In, 177Lu, and 90Y, and the 200 dpm/100 cm2 limit for alpha emitters.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: What is the maximum allowable removable surface contamination for alpha-emitting radionuclides in a restricted area?

choices.text: No specific limit; alpha emitters are assessed case by case

questions.explanation: All alpha emitters are subject to the most restrictive surface contamination limit of 200 dpm per 100 cm2. This is ten times more restrictive than the 2,000 dpm/100 cm2 limit for isotopes such as 131I and 90Y, and 100 times more restrictive than the 20,000 dpm/100 cm2 limit for 99mTc and 67Ga.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A wipe of a restricted area work surface where 131I was used reveals 2,800 dpm/100 cm2 of removable contamination. What is the appropriate response?

choices.text: Repeat the wipe in 6 hours to confirm, given 131I's decay characteristics
Notify the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) and initiate decontamination
No action required - this level is within the acceptable limit for 131I

questions.explanation: The maximum allowable removable surface contamination for 131I is 2,000 dpm/100 cm2. A level of 2,800 dpm/100 cm2 exceeds this limit and requires decontamination. The RSO should be notified, cleaning supplies assembled, the area scrubbed from the borders inward, and effectiveness monitored with wipes and portable surveys. Environmental Health and Safety should be notified upon completion for a follow-up survey.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A wipe of a surface in a restricted area where 99mTc was prepared shows 14,000 dpm/100 cm2 of removable contamination. What is the appropriate response?

choices.text: File a radioactive contamination report with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC)
Notify the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) and initiate decontamination immediately
No action required - this level is within the allowable limit for 99mTc
Restrict access to the area pending RSO evaluation

questions.explanation: The maximum allowable removable surface contamination for 99mTc is 20,000 dpm/100 cm2. A reading of 14,000 dpm/100 cm2 is below this threshold and requires no decontamination action. This contrasts with isotopes such as 131I and 90Y, for which the limit is only 2,000 dpm/100 cm2 - a level that 14,000 dpm/100 cm2 would clearly exceed.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Which of the following groupings correctly matches radionuclides to their allowable removable surface contamination limit?

choices.text: 90Y and 201Tl - same limit of 20,000 dpm/100 cm2
99mTc and 131I - same limit of 2,000 dpm/100 cm2
67Ga and 131I - same limit of 2,000 dpm/100 cm2
177Lu and 123I - same limit of 2,000 dpm/100 cm2

questions.explanation: 177Lu and 123I are both in the group with a 2,000 dpm/100 cm2 surface contamination limit, which also includes 111In, 131I, and 90Y. 99mTc belongs to the 20,000 dpm/100 cm2 group (with 67Ga and 201Tl), not the 2,000 group. 90Y is in the 2,000 group, not the 20,000 group with 201Tl. And 131I is in the 2,000 group, not the same group as 67Ga.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: When removable contamination is assessed on an object with less than 100 cm2 of total surface area, how should the measurement and limit be applied?

choices.text: Objects smaller than 100 cm2 are exempt from quantitative contamination limits
The entire surface should be wiped, and the allowable level reduced proportionally to the actual surface area
The contamination limit should be doubled to compensate for the smaller surface area
The standard 100 cm2 limit applies regardless of the object's size

questions.explanation: When the object's surface area is less than 100 cm2, the entire surface should be wiped, and the applicable contamination level should be reduced proportionally. For example, if only 50 cm2 is available, the allowable limit is halved. This ensures consistency in the contamination assessment relative to surface area.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A radiological dispersal device (RDD) differs from a nuclear bomb primarily in that:

choices.text: An RDD combines conventional explosives with radioactive material and does not produce a nuclear chain reaction
An RDD releases a radiation cloud that can spread contamination across thousands of square miles
An RDD uses highly enriched uranium while a nuclear bomb uses plutonium
An RDD is classified as a weapon of mass destruction, whereas a nuclear bomb is not

questions.explanation: A dirty bomb, or RDD, combines a conventional explosive such as dynamite with radioactive material. It does not produce a nuclear detonation or chain reaction. A nuclear bomb creates an explosion millions of times more powerful. The radiation cloud from a nuclear bomb can spread thousands of square miles, whereas an RDD's contamination is typically limited to a few blocks or miles. An RDD is classified as a weapon of mass disruption, not mass destruction - contamination and public anxiety are its primary effects.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A dirty bomb is best characterized as a weapon of mass:
questions.explanation: A dirty bomb (RDD) is explicitly described as a "weapon of mass disruption," not a weapon of mass destruction. The conventional explosive component would cause more immediate harm than the radiation. The primary objectives of an RDD are to create fear and panic, contaminate property, and require costly cleanup - not to cause mass radiation casualties.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: In a radiological emergency scenario involving an radiological dispersal device (RDD), what is the first priority?

choices.text: Assessment and treatment of any life- or limb-threatening medical conditions
Identification of the radioactive material used to guide protective actions
Decontamination of all potentially exposed individuals
Notification of federal agencies including the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and Department of Homeland Security

questions.explanation: In any accident or emergency involving radioactive materials, life- or limb-threatening medical situations must always be addressed first and foremost. Contamination control and exposure control are important but must never delay or impede medical assistance. Emergency personnel should be notified about radioactive material involvement before treatment when possible, so they can protect themselves and prevent spread - but only after ensuring the patient receives necessary care.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Which of the following factors does NOT determine the health effects of radiation exposure following an radiological dispersal device (RDD) incident?

choices.text: The amount of radiation absorbed by the body
The distance from the source of radiation to an individual
The specific brand name of the explosive device used
Whether the exposure was external or through inhalation or ingestion

questions.explanation: The health effects of radiation from an RDD are determined by: the amount of radiation absorbed, the type of radiation (gamma, beta, or alpha), the distance from the source, the means of exposure (external, inhaled, ingested, or skin absorption), and the length of time exposed. The type of explosive device used does not directly affect radiation dose. The health effects of radiation tend to be directly proportional to radiation dose.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: What is the first step when a worker experiences personal skin contamination with radioactive material?

choices.text: Notify the Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) before taking any personal action
Apply an antiseptic to prevent absorption of the radioactive material through the skin
Remove all contaminated personal protective clothing (lab coat, gloves, etc.)
Wash the contaminated area immediately with soap and water

questions.explanation: The first step in managing personal contamination is to remove all contaminated personal protective clothing, including lab coat and gloves. After removal of contaminated clothing, the area should be washed with mild soap and water, and then monitored; washing should be repeated as necessary. Notifying the RSO is important but follows the immediate personal decontamination steps.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: After removing contaminated clothing and washing a contaminated skin area with mild soap and water, what is the next step?

choices.text: Place an impermeable dressing over the area to prevent further spread
Seek immediate evaluation in the emergency department
Apply a chelating agent to bind residual radioactivity
Monitor the contaminated area and repeat washing as necessary

questions.explanation: After the initial wash, the contaminated area should be monitored to assess whether contamination remains. If it does, washing should be repeated as needed. This cycle of wash-monitor-repeat is the standard personal decontamination approach. Chelating agents and emergency department referrals are not part of the routine personal contamination protocol.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: When decontaminating a surface contaminated with radioactive material, in what direction should scrubbing proceed?

choices.text: In the direction of existing airflow to minimize aerosolization
From the borders of the contaminated area inward toward the center
From the center of the contamination outward toward the borders
In alternating directions to ensure complete coverage

questions.explanation: Decontamination scrubbing should proceed from the borders of the contaminated area inward toward the center, cleaning small areas at a time. This technique prevents spreading contamination outward to previously clean areas. Scrubbing from the center outward would carry contamination into the surrounding clean areas, worsening the situation.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: After completing decontamination of a contaminated laboratory surface, who should be notified so that a follow-up contamination survey can be performed?

choices.text: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) regional office
The authorized user who ordered the radioactive material

questions.explanation: Upon completion of the decontamination effort, Environmental Health and Safety (EHS) should be notified so that a follow-up contamination survey can be performed to verify that decontamination was effective. The Radiation Safety Officer (RSO) is notified upon discovery of the contamination (to assess extent and advise on decontamination), while EHS handles the confirmatory survey after cleanup.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Which combination of characteristics is required for an exposure to cause acute radiation syndrome?

choices.text: Any dose greater than 0.7 Gy, regardless of dose rate, body region exposed, or source
Internal contamination with a radionuclide delivering more than 0.7 Gy to the bone marrow
Acute high-dose (>0.7 Gy) exposure from external penetrating radiation at a high dose rate, involving more than 70% of the body
Whole-body radiation dose from any source (internal or external) exceeding 1 Gy

questions.explanation: Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) requires all four of the following: an acute high dose (greater than 0.7 Gy), a high dose rate delivered in a short time, external penetrating radiation (not internal emitters), and exposure of more than 70% of the body. A dose of 0.7 Gy from an internal emitter would not produce ARS because the source is internal, not external. Partial-body exposures, even at high doses, would not cause classical ARS if less than 70% of the body is involved.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: What is the minimum whole-body absorbed dose from external penetrating radiation required to cause acute radiation syndrome?
questions.explanation: Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) requires an acute high dose exceeding 0.7 Gy. This threshold also corresponds to the lower boundary of the hematopoietic subsyndrome dose range. At doses below 0.7 Gy, even with whole-body penetrating external exposure, classic ARS does not develop. The 0.5 Gy value is near the threshold but does not meet the criterion; 0.1 Gy is far below the threshold.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A worker is exposed to 1.5 Gy of penetrating radiation delivered to the lower half of the body only. Which of the following best describes the expected outcome?

choices.text: Hematopoietic subsyndrome of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS), since the dose exceeds 0.7 Gy
ARS would not be expected, because the dose does not exceed the 3.5 Gy lethal threshold
ARS would not be expected, because less than 70% of the body was exposed
Full acute radiation syndrome, including prodromal, latent, and manifest illness phases

questions.explanation: ARS requires exposure of more than 70% of the body. Exposure confined to the lower half of the body represents approximately 50% body involvement and therefore does not meet this criterion. ARS would not be expected to develop, even though the dose of 1.5 Gy would otherwise be sufficient. The 3.5 Gy value is the LD50/60 without treatment, not the threshold for ARS.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A patient exposed to a high whole-body radiation dose initially presents with nausea, vomiting, and fever, then appears to improve and feel normal for several days before deteriorating again. The period of apparent improvement corresponds to which phase of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS)?
questions.explanation: The latent phase is characterized by reduced or no symptoms - a period of apparent recovery between the initial prodromal symptoms and the onset of manifest illness. With increasing radiation doses, this latent interval shortens. The prodromal phase is the early symptomatic period (nausea, vomiting, fever, etc.), and manifest illness is the later phase when dose-dependent subsyndrome symptoms emerge.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Which of the following is a symptom associated with the prodromal phase of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS)?
questions.explanation: The prodromal phase is characterized by nausea and vomiting, headache, diarrhea, fever, and loss of consciousness. The other choices (bone marrow failure, hemorrhagic stroke, GI bleeding, and sepsis) are manifestations of the manifest illness phase, corresponding to specific ARS subsyndromes - hematopoietic, neurovascular, and gastrointestinal, respectively.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: How does the time course of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) change with increasing radiation dose?

choices.text: The phases lengthen, giving the body more time to recover between stages
The phases shorten and symptoms worsen
The prodromal phase is eliminated entirely at very high doses
The latent phase extends at higher doses, making clinical monitoring more challenging

questions.explanation: With increasing radiation doses, the time interval for each phase of ARS is shortened and the symptoms worsen. In other words, higher doses compress the timeline - the prodromal phase occurs sooner, the latent phase is briefer, and manifest illness develops more rapidly and severely. Answer D is the opposite of what occurs.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: In the manifest illness phase of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS), symptoms are best characterized as:

choices.text: Identical to prodromal symptoms but more severe
Dependent on the absorbed dose, grouped into distinct subsyndromes based on organ system involvement
Uniform across all patients regardless of the dose received
Primarily neurological in all cases, regardless of total dose

questions.explanation: During the manifest illness phase, symptoms are dose-dependent and correspond to the ARS subsyndrome associated with the organ system or cell type most critically injured. Lower doses produce hematopoietic subsyndrome, higher doses produce gastrointestinal subsyndrome, and the highest doses produce neurovascular subsyndrome. The character of illness is not uniform and varies based on the radiation dose.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: The recovery/death phase of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) may include which of the following long-term outcomes?

choices.text: Permanent hematopoietic failure requiring lifelong transfusion support in all survivors
Stochastic effects, deterministic effects, or death, depending on dose and treatment
Complete resolution of all radiation-related effects within 30 days
Full recovery in all survivors without long-term sequelae if supportive care was provided

questions.explanation: The recovery or death phase can result in recovery, or long-term effects including stochastic effects (such as increased cancer risk) and deterministic effects (such as organ damage). At sufficiently high doses and without adequate treatment, death may occur. The outcome is not uniformly favorable even with supportive care, and varies substantially with dose.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: At what dose range does the hematopoietic subsyndrome of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) manifest?
questions.explanation: The hematopoietic subsyndrome develops at whole-body doses of 0.7 to 5 Gy. It is characterized by bone marrow failure and pancytopenia. At higher doses (6 to 9 Gy), the gastrointestinal subsyndrome predominates; above 10 Gy, the neurovascular subsyndrome occurs. The 0.7 Gy lower boundary also corresponds to the minimum dose threshold for ARS overall.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: At what dose range does the gastrointestinal subsyndrome of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) manifest?
questions.explanation: The gastrointestinal subsyndrome develops at whole-body doses of 6 to 9 Gy and results from gastrointestinal stem cell toxicity. Characteristic findings include severe gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms, GI bleeding, electrolyte abnormalities, and sepsis. The 0.7 to 5 Gy range corresponds to the hematopoietic subsyndrome, and greater than 10 Gy corresponds to the neurovascular subsyndrome.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Above what whole-body dose does the neurovascular subsyndrome of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) occur?
questions.explanation: The neurovascular subsyndrome manifests at whole-body doses greater than 10 Gy and results from neurovascular endothelial cell toxicity. It is the most severe of the three ARS subsyndromes and is characterized by hemorrhagic stroke, loss of consciousness, and decreased blood pressure. At this dose level, survival without intensive intervention is unlikely.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department following a radiation accident. In the manifest illness phase, the patient develops pancytopenia and evidence of bone marrow failure. Which Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) subsyndrome is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow failure and pancytopenia are the hallmark findings of the hematopoietic subsyndrome, which occurs at doses of 0.7 to 5 Gy and reflects bone marrow toxicity. The gastrointestinal subsyndrome (6 to 9 Gy) presents with severe gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms, GI bleeding, electrolyte abnormalities, and sepsis. The neurovascular subsyndrome (greater than 10 Gy) presents with hemorrhagic stroke, loss of consciousness, and hypotension.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A radiation accident victim in the manifest illness phase presents with hemorrhagic stroke, loss of consciousness, and hypotension. Which subsyndrome and approximate minimum whole-body dose does this represent?
questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic stroke, loss of consciousness, and decreased blood pressure are characteristic of the neurovascular subsyndrome, which results from neurovascular endothelial cell toxicity at doses greater than 10 Gy. This is the most severe Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) subsyndrome. The gastrointestinal subsyndrome (6 to 9 Gy) causes gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding and sepsis, and the hematopoietic subsyndrome (0.7 to 5 Gy) causes bone marrow failure and pancytopenia.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: A radiation accident victim is estimated to have received a whole-body dose of approximately 8 Gy. During the manifest illness phase, which subsyndrome is most expected to predominate?

choices.text: Hematopoietic subsyndrome - bone marrow failure and pancytopenia
Gastrointestinal subsyndrome - gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding, electrolyte abnormalities, and sepsis
Neurovascular subsyndrome - hemorrhagic stroke and hypotension

questions.explanation: A whole-body dose of 8 Gy falls within the gastrointestinal subsyndrome range (6 to 9 Gy). This subsyndrome is caused by gastrointestinal stem cell toxicity and is characterized by severe GI symptoms, GI bleeding, electrolyte abnormalities, and sepsis. The hematopoietic subsyndrome occurs at 0.7 to 5 Gy, and the neurovascular subsyndrome occurs above 10 Gy.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly lists the three Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) subsyndromes in order of increasing dose threshold?
questions.explanation: The ARS subsyndromes occur in order of increasing dose: hematopoietic (0.7 to 5 Gy), gastrointestinal (6 to 9 Gy), and neurovascular (greater than 10 Gy). As the dose increases, higher-order systems are injured in addition to the bone marrow. Understanding this sequence is important for both prognostication and treatment planning.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Without medical intervention, what is the estimated LD50/60 for acute whole-body low-LET irradiation?
questions.explanation: The LD50/60 - the dose at which 50% of an exposed population would die within 60 days - is estimated at 3.5 to 4 Gy for acute whole-body low-LET radiation without any medical intervention. This improves substantially with treatment. With antibiotics and supportive care, the LD50/60 rises to 4.5 to 7 Gy; with intensive care, reverse isolation, and hematopoietic cell transplantation, it can potentially reach 7 to 9 Gy.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Administration of antibiotics and supportive care following acute whole-body radiation exposure raises the LD50/60 to approximately:
questions.explanation: With the addition of antibiotics and supportive treatment, the LD50/60 for acute whole-body radiation rises from the untreated estimate of 3.5 to 4 Gy to approximately 4.5 to 7 Gy. Further escalation to intensive care, reverse isolation, and hematopoietic cell transplantation can potentially raise the LD50/60 to 7 to 9 Gy. The 3.5 to 4 Gy range represents the untreated baseline.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: With intensive care, reverse isolation, and hematopoietic cell transplantation, the LD50/60 for acute whole-body radiation can potentially be raised to:
questions.explanation: The most aggressive treatment - intensive care, reverse isolation, and hematopoietic cell transplantation - can potentially raise the LD50/60 to 7 to 9 Gy. This compares to 4.5 to 7 Gy with antibiotics and supportive care only, and 3.5 to 4 Gy with no intervention. Despite this improvement, historical data on stem cell transplantation for Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) treatment are limited and mixed, with a low and questionable success rate.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved colony-stimulating factors (CSFs) for the treatment of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) primarily target which subsyndrome?
questions.explanation: The FDA-approved CSFs for ARS treatment - filgrastim, PEGylated filgrastim, and sargramostim - predominantly target the hematopoietic subsyndrome by promoting bone marrow recovery, particularly neutrophil production. New treatments are under investigation for the gastrointestinal subsyndrome as well, but currently approved therapies are focused on hematopoietic recovery.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Which of the following is an Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved colony-stimulating factor for the treatment of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS)?
questions.explanation: Sargramostim (Leukine) is an FDA-approved granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (Geiger-Mueller (GM)-colony-stimulating factor (CSF)) for ARS treatment. The other approved CSFs are filgrastim (Neupogen) and PEGylated filgrastim (Neulasta). Romiplostim (Nplate) is also FDA-approved for ARS but is a thrombopoietin receptor activator, not a CSF. Epoetin alfa and darbepoetin alfa promote red blood cell production and are not approved for ARS.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Which Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) treatment promotes recovery of neutrophils as well as additional bone marrow cell lineages beyond the neutrophil lineage?
questions.explanation: All three approved CSFs promote neutrophil recovery, but sargramostim (Leukine) additionally promotes other bone marrow cell lineages. Filgrastim and PEGylated filgrastim are granulocyte colony-stimulating factors (G-CSFs) that primarily drive neutrophil production. Romiplostim is a thrombopoietin receptor activator that promotes megakaryocytes and platelets, not neutrophils.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action of romiplostim (Nplate) in the treatment of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS)?

choices.text: Thrombopoietin receptor activator that promotes megakaryocyte and platelet recovery
Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor that promotes multiple bone marrow lineages
Erythropoietin receptor agonist that drives red blood cell production
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor that accelerates neutrophil recovery

questions.explanation: Romiplostim (Nplate) is a thrombopoietin (TPO) receptor activator approved for ARS treatment. It promotes megakaryocyte production and platelet recovery - the platelet lineage that is critically depleted in hematopoietic ARS. Filgrastim and PEGylated filgrastim are G-CSFs (neutrophil-focused), and sargramostim is a Geiger-Mueller (GM)-colony-stimulating factor (CSF) (multiple lineages including neutrophils). Erythropoietin-class agents are not approved for ARS.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved colony-stimulating factor for Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) treatment?
questions.explanation: Romiplostim (Nplate) is FDA-approved for ARS treatment, but it is a thrombopoietin receptor activator - not a colony-stimulating factor. The three FDA-approved CSFs for ARS are filgrastim (Neupogen), PEGylated filgrastim (Neulasta), and sargramostim (Leukine). Romiplostim targets megakaryocytes and platelets, while the CSFs target neutrophil (and for sargramostim, additional) bone marrow lineages.

questions.chapterName: Section 7: Emergency Procedures, Accidents/Incidents, and Special Circumstances
questions.stem: Historical data on the use of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) treatment demonstrates:

choices.text: Limited and mixed results with a low and questionable success rate
Reliable effectiveness when performed within 72 hours of exposure
Superiority over colony-stimulating factors alone in patients with doses above 5 Gy
High success rates, making it the preferred treatment for severe hematopoietic subsyndrome

questions.explanation: Although hematopoietic cell transplantation might seem like a logical treatment for the bone marrow failure of hematopoietic ARS, historical data are limited and mixed, with a very low and questionable success rate. Despite this, intensive care protocols that include reverse isolation and transplantation can potentially raise the LD50/60 to 7 to 9 Gy - an improvement over supportive care alone, though transplantation's specific contribution remains uncertain.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: What are the two main structural components of a Geiger-Mueller counter?

choices.text: An ionization chamber and a scintillation crystal
A sealed gas-filled tube and an information display
A lead collimator and a sodium iodide detector
A photomultiplier tube and a multichannel analyzer

questions.explanation: A Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter has two main parts: a sealed tube (or chamber) filled with gas, and an information display. Radiation enters the tube, creates ion pairs in the gas, and the resulting current is conveyed to the display as a needle deflection or numeric readout. A photomultiplier tube and multichannel analyzer are components of a well counter; an ionization chamber is a separate instrument type.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: How does a Geiger-Mueller counter detect radiation?

choices.text: Radiation interacts with a thin-layer chromatography plate, separating radioactive species by mobility
It measures the total charge accumulated on two conducting electrodes proportional to the number of ions
It measures the energy deposited by radiation in a scintillating crystal, producing a flash of light
Radiation entering the gas-filled tube creates ion pairs; electrons are attracted to a central wire, generating a measurable current

questions.explanation: In a Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter, radiation enters the sealed gas-filled tube and collides with gas atoms, pushing electrons away to create ion pairs. A wire in the middle of the tube attracts these electrons, creating additional ion pairs and sending a current to the information display. The output is typically expressed as counts per minute - the number of ion pairs created every 60 seconds.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: What information does a Geiger-Mueller counter provide about detected radiation?

choices.text: The absorbed dose rate in the tissue of interest
The specific radionuclide responsible for the detected activity
An indication that an ion pair was created, but no information about radiation type or energy
The type of radiation (alpha, beta, or gamma) and its energy

questions.explanation: A Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter indicates when an ion pair is created - registering a count - but provides no information about the type of radiation or its energy. It cannot distinguish alpha from beta from gamma radiation, and cannot identify the specific radionuclide. For energy-selective or isotope-specific counting, instruments such as a well counter with a multichannel analyzer are required.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: The output of a Geiger-Mueller counter is expressed as counts per minute (CPM). What does one count represent?

choices.text: One ion pair created in the gas-filled tube during a 60-second interval
The absorbed dose from one disintegration of a radioactive atom
The total energy deposited by one radiation event in the detector
One photon detected by the photomultiplier tube per minute

questions.explanation: Each count on a Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter represents the detection of one ion pair created in the gas-filled tube. Counts per minute refers to the number of such ion pairs created every 60 seconds. The GM counter does not measure energy deposition per event, absorbed dose, or photon flux directly - it simply counts ionization events.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: Well counters are best suited for which of the following applications?

choices.text: High-sensitivity counting of radioactive specimens such as blood, urine, or wipe samples
Measuring patient dose rates at 1 meter following radiopharmaceutical administration
Continuous real-time monitoring of airborne radioactivity in a laboratory
Measuring ambient dose rates in a restricted area during routine facility surveys

questions.explanation: Well counters are designed for high-sensitivity counting of radioactive specimens - including blood or urine samples and wipes from removable contamination surveys (wipe testing). Their high intrinsic and geometric efficiency makes them ideal for measuring very low activity specimens. They are not used for ambient area surveys, patient release dose rate measurements, or airborne monitoring.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: What scintillation crystal is most commonly used in a well counter?
questions.explanation: The most commonly used scintillation crystal in a well counter is thallium-doped sodium iodide - NaI(Tl). The crystal has a cylindrical shape with a circular bore (well) into which the sample is placed, and is backed by a photomultiplier tube and associated electronics. The well geometry maximizes geometric efficiency by surrounding the sample on multiple sides.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: What component of a modern well counter enables energy-selective (isotope-specific) counting?
questions.explanation: A multichannel analyzer (MCA) sorts detected events by energy, enabling the counter to distinguish between radionuclides based on their photon energies. This allows for isotope-selective counting and can determine the specific radionuclide responsible for contamination. The PMT converts light pulses to electrical signals, the sample changer allows unattended multi-sample counting, and the well geometry improves geometric efficiency - but energy discrimination is the function of the MCA.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: What is the maximum activity at which a well counter can reliably measure samples without significant counting error?
questions.explanation: Well counters can reliably be used only for counting activities up to approximately 37 kBq (0.001 mCi). At higher activities, dead-time counting losses become prohibitive and the measured counts become inaccurate. Dead time refers to the brief period after each detected event during which the detector cannot register another event; at high count rates, a significant fraction of true events are missed.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: Why does a well counter become inaccurate at high sample activities?

choices.text: The photomultiplier tube saturates and produces a constant output regardless of activity
Dead-time counting losses become prohibitive, causing the measured counts to underestimate true activity
The NaI(Tl) crystal begins to phosphoresce, adding background counts unrelated to the sample
The multichannel analyzer cannot process more than one energy window simultaneously at high count rates

questions.explanation: At activities above approximately 37 kBq (0.001 mCi), dead-time counting losses become prohibitive. Dead time is the brief interval after each detected event during which the detector is unable to register another event. At high count rates, many true events occur during these dead-time intervals and go undetected, causing the measured count rate to significantly underestimate the true activity of the sample.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: The high sensitivity of a well counter results from two geometric and material factors. Which of the following correctly identifies both?

choices.text: The use of a photomultiplier tube (PMT) and a multichannel analyzer operating in coincidence
The use of a lead collimator and a high-purity germanium crystal
The use of a thin crystal and a flat-plate counting geometry
The use of a thick crystal and a well-type counting geometry

questions.explanation: The well counter achieves its high sensitivity through two factors: the use of a thick scintillation crystal (providing high intrinsic efficiency - the probability that a photon entering the crystal will interact and be detected) and a well-type counting geometry (providing high geometric efficiency - the fraction of emitted radiation that enters the detector). Together, these result in extremely high overall counting efficiency for low-activity specimens.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: What is the fundamental detection principle of a scintillation detection system?

choices.text: Ionizing radiation deposits charge on two conducting electrodes, and the accumulated charge is measured
Ionizing radiation interacts with a substance that produces a flash of light, which is then converted to an electrical signal
Ionizing radiation separates radioactive species on a chromatography plate based on their mobility
Ionizing radiation creates ion pairs in a gas, which generate a measurable electric current

questions.explanation: Scintillation detection systems work by using a material - the scintillator - that produces a flash of light when ionizing radiation interacts with it. This light is then converted to an electrical signal (typically by a photomultiplier tube). This principle differs from gas ionization (used in Geiger-Mueller (GM) counters and ionization chambers) and from chromatographic separation (used in radio-thin-layer chromatography (TLC)).

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: Liquid scintillation counting is most appropriate for measuring which type of radioactive samples?

choices.text: Ambient gamma dose rates in restricted areas
Low-level radioactivity from particulate (alpha and beta) emitting samples
Sealed sources requiring routine leak testing
High-energy gamma emitters requiring precise energy discrimination

questions.explanation: Liquid scintillation counting is an analytical technique used to identify and quantify low levels of radioactivity, particularly from particulate-emitting (beta and alpha) radioactive samples. It is also used for contamination assessment. Because alpha and beta particles cannot penetrate most detector housings, immersing the sample directly in liquid scintillant allows efficient detection of particulate emitters that would otherwise be difficult to measure externally.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: What type of radiation are solid scintillation detectors primarily sensitive to, and what dose rate range can they measure?

choices.text: Neutron radiation; millirem per hour range
Beta radiation; millirem per hour range
Alpha radiation; nanogray per hour range
Gamma radiation; microrem per hour range

questions.explanation: Solid scintillators are sensitive to gamma radiation and can measure dose rates in the microrem per hour (µrem/hr) range - making them highly sensitive instruments suitable for detecting very low gamma dose rates. This sensitivity distinguishes solid scintillation detectors from Geiger-Mueller (GM) counters, which are typically used at higher count rates and do not provide direct dose rate measurement in the µrem/hr range.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: What quantity does an ionization chamber directly measure?

choices.text: The light output produced when radiation interacts with the detector material
The count rate of radioactive disintegrations per minute
The number of ions within the gas-filled medium between the electrodes
The energy of individual radiation events

questions.explanation: An ionization chamber measures the number of ions produced within the gas-filled medium between its two conducting electrodes (anode and cathode). When radiation ionizes the gas, the resulting ions and free electrons migrate to the electrodes, creating a measurable current. The accumulated charge is proportional to the number of ions produced, which in turn reflects the radiation dose.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: In an ionization chamber, the charge accumulated on each electrode is proportional to which of the following?

choices.text: The energy of the incident radiation only, regardless of the number of ionization events
The number of like-charged ions that deposit or remove charge from that electrode
The voltage applied across the electrodes, independent of radiation exposure
The atomic number of the gas used to fill the chamber

questions.explanation: Each ion in the chamber deposits or removes a small electric charge to or from an electrode. The total accumulated charge is therefore proportional to the number of like-charged ions - which reflects the total ionization produced by the radiation. This proportional relationship between charge and ionization is what allows ionization chambers to provide accurate dose measurements.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: Open ionization chambers are typically used for which application?

choices.text: Measuring ambient gamma dose rates in the µrem/hr range
Measuring the activity of radiopharmaceutical doses prior to administration
Counting radioactive wipe samples in the laboratory

questions.explanation: Open ionization chambers are typically used as personal dosimeters - devices worn by radiation workers to measure and record their occupational radiation exposure. Sealed ionization chambers, by contrast, are used as radioisotope dose calibrators in nuclear medicine. Wipe sample counting is performed with well counters, and µrem/hr-range gamma measurements are performed with solid scintillation detectors.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: A radioisotope dose calibrator is best described as which type of instrument?

choices.text: A sealed ionization chamber calibrated to specific isotopes, providing output proportional to radiation dose
A Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter modified to measure activity in millicuries
A solid scintillation detector with a multichannel analyzer for isotope identification
An open ionization chamber calibrated to measure ambient dose rate

questions.explanation: Radioisotope dose calibrators are sealed ionization chambers widely used in nuclear medicine and the nuclear industry. They provide an output that is proportional to radiation dose and are calibrated to specific isotopes, allowing direct readout of activity (e.g., in mCi or MBq) for the isotope selected. Unlike open ionization chambers (personal dosimeters), dose calibrators are sealed to control the gas composition and pressure.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly matches an ionization chamber type to its primary use?

choices.text: Both open and sealed ionization chambers are used interchangeably for personal dosimetry and dose calibration
Open ionization chamber - radiopharmaceutical dose calibration
Open ionization chamber - personal dosimetry; sealed ionization chamber - dose calibration

questions.explanation: Open ionization chambers are used as personal dosimeters worn by radiation workers to record occupational exposure. Sealed ionization chambers are used as radioisotope dose calibrators in nuclear medicine, where they provide activity readouts calibrated to specific isotopes. The distinction between open and sealed configurations reflects their different applications and operating environments.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: Radio-thin-layer chromatography (radio-thin-layer chromatography (TLC)) is primarily used in nuclear medicine for which purpose?

choices.text: Separating gamma-emitting isotopes from beta-emitting isotopes in a mixed waste stream
Counting removable surface contamination from wipe samples
Analyzing the radiochemical purity of radiopharmaceuticals or determining reaction conversion during radiosynthesis
Measuring the dose rate from a prepared radiopharmaceutical dose at 1 meter

questions.explanation: Radio-TLC is commonly used to analyze the radiochemical purity of radiopharmaceuticals - that is, the fraction of total radioactivity that is in the desired chemical form. It is also used to determine reaction conversion when optimizing radiosynthesis processes. It does not measure dose rates, count contamination wipes (that is done with a well counter), or separate isotopes by decay mode.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: In which situation is radio-thin-layer chromatography (TLC) preferred over radio-high-performance liquid chromatography (radio-high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC))?

choices.text: When many different radioactive species are present and precise separation of all components is needed
When there are few radioactive species, because radio-TLC is simpler and provides quicker analysis
When the radiopharmaceutical contains only alpha-emitting species, which cannot be detected by HPLC
When the sample activity exceeds 37 kBq, because radio-HPLC is limited to low-activity samples

questions.explanation: Radio-TLC is preferred over radio-HPLC in applications where there are few radioactive species, because of its simplicity and relatively quick analysis time. When multiple species require precise separation and quantification, radio-HPLC may be necessary. The activity limitation of 37 kBq applies to well counters, not to radio-HPLC. Alpha detection capability is not the basis for choosing between TLC and HPLC.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: Radio-thin-layer chromatography (TLC) methodology was developed primarily as an extension of which earlier technique?
questions.explanation: Most approaches to radio-TLC were extensions or modifications of techniques previously used in paper chromatography (PC). Both techniques rely on the differential migration of chemical species along a stationary phase, with the mobile phase carrying components at different rates based on their chemical properties. Radio-TLC adapted this principle to the analysis of radioactive compounds.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: A nuclear medicine technologist needs to verify the radiochemical purity of a freshly prepared 99mTc radiopharmaceutical before patient administration. Which instrument is most appropriate?

choices.text: Radio-thin-layer chromatography (TLC) with an appropriate detector

questions.explanation: Radiochemical purity - the fraction of total radioactivity present in the desired chemical form - is determined by radio-TLC (or radio-high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)). The dose calibrator measures total activity of the dose but cannot distinguish between different chemical species. The Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter detects radiation but cannot separate or identify chemical forms. The well counter is used for low-activity specimen counting, not radiochemical purity analysis.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: A wipe of a work surface yields a sample that needs to be counted for removable contamination. The expected activity on the wipe is very low. Which instrument is most appropriate?

choices.text: Solid scintillation detector in the µrem/hr range
Geiger-Mueller counter used in survey mode

questions.explanation: Well counters are specifically designed for high-sensitivity counting of wipe samples from removable contamination surveys. Their high intrinsic and geometric efficiency make them ideal for quantifying very low activities on wipe samples. The Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter is used for area surveys but is less sensitive than a well counter for specimen counting. The dose calibrator is designed for measuring radiopharmaceutical doses, not wipe samples.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: Which of the following instruments can identify the specific radionuclide responsible for detected contamination?

choices.text: Well counter equipped with a multichannel analyzer

questions.explanation: A well counter equipped with a multichannel analyzer (MCA) can perform energy-selective counting and thereby identify the specific radionuclide present in a sample based on its characteristic photon energy. A Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter detects ion pairs but provides no energy or identity information. A personal dosimeter measures cumulative exposure but cannot identify specific isotopes. A dose calibrator measures total activity of a known isotope (selected by the operator) but does not independently identify unknown radionuclides.

questions.chapterName: Appendix 1: Radiation-Measuring Instrumentation and Quality Control Tests
questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs each instrument with its primary detection mechanism?

choices.text: GM counter - charge accumulation; well counter - scintillation; ionization chamber - gas ionization
Geiger-Mueller (GM) counter - scintillation; well counter - gas ionization; ionization chamber - charge accumulation
GM counter - gas ionization; well counter - scintillation; ionization chamber - charge accumulation
GM counter - scintillation; well counter - charge accumulation; ionization chamber - scintillation

questions.explanation: The GM counter detects radiation through gas ionization - radiation creates ion pairs in a gas-filled tube, and the resulting current is measured. The well counter uses scintillation - a NaI(Tl) crystal produces light flashes when struck by gamma photons, which are converted to electrical pulses by a photomultiplier tube (PMT). The ionization chamber also uses gas ionization, but measures the total accumulated charge proportional to the number of ions, providing a dose-proportional output rather than individual counts.
